title: The 37 biggest Lego sets ever made
content:
From conversation-starting display pieces to towering monuments, this up-to-date guide tracks the biggest Lego sets ever made. We can help you find rare behemoths to add to your collection, and we also list the newest additions to Lego's giant hall of fame.

For clarity, we're measuring Lego sets with the most pieces, not merely those with grand physical dimensions. Unsurprisingly, these ultra-large sets also include some of the most expensive Lego sets on the market - but size is no guarantee of quality: if you want our all time favorites, try our guide to the best Lego sets instead.

These are the biggest Lego sets: 

  • Lego World Map
  • Lego Eiffel Tower
  • Lego Titanic
  • Lego Colosseum
  • Lego Millennium Falcon UCS
  • Lego AT AT Walker UCS
  • Lego Razor Crest
  • Lego Rivendell
  • Ninjago City Markets
  • Lego Hogwarts Castle
  • Lego Taj Mahal
  • Lego Santiago Bernabeu
  • Ninjago City Gardens
  • Lego Diagon Alley
  • Lego Camp Nou
  • Lego Barad Dur
  • Lego Venator
  • Lego Avengers Tower
  • 2007 UCS Millennium Falcon
  • Lego Hogwarts Express
  • Lego Ninjago City
  • The Old Town
  • Lego Disney Castle
  • Lego Gringotts Wizarding Bank
  • UCS Star Destroyer
  • Lego Mosaic Maker
  • Lego Ghostbusters Firehouse
  • Lego Lion Knights Castle
  • Lego Notre Dame
  • Lego Tower Bridge
  • Lego Harry Potter Hogwarts Crests
  • Gotham City
  • Jim Lee Batman Lego Collection
  • Tropical Aquarium
  • River Steamboat
  • Natural History Museum
  • Gustav Klimt The Kiss
  • FAQs

Lego World Map

ID code 31203
Number of pieces 11,695
Minifigures included 0

Released in June 2021, the Lego Art World Map contains 11,695 pieces, making it the biggest Lego set ever made. Much more a piece of home decor than a typical model or plaything, it's over one meter wide and is designed to be built in a color combination of your choice. You can paint the oceans of the world in pastel colors, create patterns in the seas, or build a monochrome map.

Using a nifty system of connectors, you can even choose which continent lies at the map's center. But it's not only something to look at. Mark your travels across the globe by dotting small, colored pins on the countries you've visited, or listen to the included soundtrack to take an audio tour.

Lego Eiffel Tower

Set number 10307
Number of pieces 10,001
Minifigures included 0

At an appropriately towering 59" (149cm), the Lego Eiffel Tower must be the toy firm's most imposing set yet. At 10,001 parts, Lego's interpretation of the Parisian landmark might not quite trump the Art World Map, but it certainly feels bigger in the room.

And if you're an engineering, history, or construction geek, you might be as thrilled as us to learn that the build process and ordering of this Lego set replicates how the original Eiffel Tower was put together - largely as a four-part process.

And the plastic Eiffel Tower isn't only about its scale and construction. It drips with elegant style and classy details, from the undersized trees down below to the flourishes on the spire at the top. If you've got the space and cash, few sets compare to the Lego Eiffel Tower.

Lego Titanic

Set number 10294
Number of pieces 9,090
Minifigures included 0

Another 2021 release, the Lego Titanic is made of 9,090 individual pieces. Although a little smaller than the real ship, it's no less impressive, and its 135-centimeter length makes it the longest Lego set ever released.

Aside from showcasing the Titanic's major external features - main deck, four smokestacks, and even its swimming pool - it also includes a detailed cross-section of the ship, letting you view the grand staircase and boiler rooms inside. With an adjustable anchor and moving engine, this is one of the more interactive big Lego sets.

Lego Colosseum

Set number 10276
Number of pieces 9,036
Minifigures included 0

Is any monument of history more impressive than the Colosseum? Probably not. Is it even more impressive when made out of Lego? Quite possibly. At 9,036 pieces, the Lego Colosseum only just comes under the Titanic, but its detail of the historical Roman ruin is unmatched.

Its perimeter includes several shades of Lego brick to capture the changing color and age of the amphitheater, while several sections can be removed to reveal the hidden passageways beneath the arena's floor. Just the shape of the model makes it truly impressive to behold.

Lego Millennium Falcon UCS

Set number 75192
Number of pieces 7,541
Minifigures included 0

On its release in 2017, the Ultimate Collector Series Millennium Falcon was the largest and highest priced Lego set ever produced. Now, its 7,541 pieces might pale in comparison to the sets above, but its detail is no less impressive. This is Han Solo's YT-1300 light freighter like you've never seen it before.

We called it one of the best Star Wars Lego sets ever produced, and it's not hard to see why. Every inch of the model is packed with detail, whether it's the removable hull panels, the interior engine room with added hyperdrive, or the main cockpit. This isn't just a large Lego set, it's an homage to perhaps the most iconic spaceship in all of science fiction.

Lego AT AT Walker UCS

Set number 75313
Number of pieces 6,785
Minifigures included 9

Since The Empire Strikes Back came out in 1980, the lumbering grey AT-AT has plodded from the icy plains of Hoth and into our hearts.

At 6,785 pieces, Lego's Ultimate Collector Series AT-AT Walker is quite a bit smaller than the Millennium Falcon in terms of sheer bricks, but a lot taller. Standing 62cm off your table, it's also fully poseable, making it one of the largest and, surprisingly, most agile sets out there. It's also one of the highest priced kits available - but if you were after cheap Lego sets, you probably wouldn't be perusing this guide.

What's most impressive about this set, however, is its relative scale. It's a perfect fit for the ordinary Lego minifigures, and the crew of Snowtroopers and pilots that come with the model only reinforce its gargantuan size.

To see Luke Skywalker tangle below the AT-AT's hull on a cable makes you realize what the Rebellion was up against. 40 whole minifigures can fit into the walker's hull, making it a real miniature mover!

Lego Razor Crest

Set number 75331
Number of pieces 6,187
Minifigures included 5

That's right, the Lego Razor Crest is the third Star Wars set in the top ten. That's testament to the fact the Star Wars Lego theme is thriving; popular enough to have plenty of fans willing to invest in sets costing hundreds of dollars. You'll need plenty of cash to invest in the 6,187-part Razor - but what a remarkable set.

It's certainly large. In fact, it's considerably weighty. It captures the Mandalorian vessel in a strikingly stylish way, and it drips with detail both inside and out. Get under the cover and it's riddled with themed rooms and nods to the TV show realized through smart building techniques.

This giant really does hit all four of the key Lego offerings: a riveting build process; loads of playability; handsome display chops; and a part supply to let you build so many other wonderful things.

Lego Rivendell

Set number 10316
Number of pieces 6,167
Minifigures included 15

As Lord of the Rings locations go, very few can convey the beauty, intricacy, tranquility, history, and otherworldliness of Tolkien's elves quite like the House of Elrond at Rivendell - and 2023's Lego Lord of the Rings Rivendell set does a surprisingly good job of capturing it in brick form.

Its sheer size and scale are part of the reason it's so beloved. It's made of several detachable sections, and each is loaded with little references that'll make LOTR fans' hearts sing.

From Bilbo's writing room, to Frodo in bed after being stabbed with the Witch-King's Morgul blade, to the statuary chamber where the shards of Narsil were kept, to the forge where they were remade into Andúril, Flame of the West… it's a lot.

A generous helping of 15 Lego minifigures sweetens the deal further, including all nine members of the Fellowship of the Ring, plus Elrond, Arwen, and Bilbo (and some no-names). The minifigs have detachable legs, too, so you can sit them around the table, re-enact the Council of Elrond, and say 'One does not simply walk into Mordor' in a Sean Bean voice! You know, er, if you want.

Ninjago City Markets

Set number 71799
Number of pieces 6,163
Minifigures included 21

After the 2021 Ninjago City Gardens set proved so popular (read about it below), it seemed inevitable we'd get another gigantic playset bringing part of Lego's futuristic East Asian-style setting to life - and so we have!

Released in 2023, Ninjago City Markets is that set, and it's both big and beautiful. Designed to complement the Gardens, it trades that set's bewildering verticality for more breadth, overall volume, and interactive doodads.

This thing has a moving cable car, elevators, various teeny room environments built into multi-level buildings - and a toilet that you can flush poop down, and the poop comes out into the river. And, to populate this veritable utopia of plumbed-in pleasures, the set includes an incredible 21 minifigures - more than any other set on this list.

At $369.99 (£319.99), it still ain't cheap, but it's among the more affordable here. If you're into the Ninjago aesthetic, and like having a lot of in-universe minifigs to play out scenarios with, this is a brilliant pick.

Lego Hogwarts Castle

Set number 71043
Number of pieces 6,020
Minifigures included 4

Although packing 6,020 pieces, the most interesting aspect of the Lego Hogwarts Castle isn't how many bricks are in the box, but the scale of the model they're used to build.

A micro-scale model, that's built to fit tiny figures instead of the usual minifigure size, Lego's cottoned on to a neat trick here; rather than a humongous Hogwarts that no den could fit, we get a medium Hogwarts and with a cast of scaled down wizards (plus some bonus minifigures for good measure).

It pays off, though. The set captures all the majesty of the famous fictional castle, containing several classic locations of the franchise: the Great Hall, the Whomping Willow, Hagrid's Hut, and the Chamber of Secrets.

Lego Taj Mahal

A huge, iconic Creator Expert set.

Set number 10256
Number of pieces 5,923
Minifigures included 0

Between 2008 and 2011, the Lego Taj Mahal was the biggest Lego set of all time. Packing 5,923 pieces, it's still a mammoth build even now. It's got symmetry, majesty, and an absolutely cracking dome at its center - the Lego design team sure know how to pick them. The Taj Mahal works brilliantly as a Lego set, and vice versa.

You won't find it in any stores, however. After briefly reappearing in 2017, the set was discontinued. Look for this one in second-hand stores or online Lego marketplaces and trading platforms, and expect to pay a real premium!

Lego Santiago Bernabéu

The biggest sports set ever.

ID code 10299
Number of pieces 5,876
Minifigures included 0

Lego Real Madrid - Santiago Bernabéu Stadium is a must-have for soccer fans. It's a huge, detailed recreation of the iconic stadium, and viewing it gets even better when you remove the top and check out the interior.

Like many symmetrical Lego sets, building the stadium can get fairly same-y. However, if you're the kind of person who finds repetition relaxing, this will be a soothing build, without too much complexity. And the final result is well worth the work.

Ninjago City Gardens

ID code 71741
Number of pieces 5,685
Minifigures included 19

Released in early 2021 in celebration of the show's tenth anniversary, Ninjago City Gardens is a three-storey slice of Ninjago City that contains many of the characters and locations fans will be familiar with from the Ninjago cartoon. And that's the main draw that makes this one of the best Ninjago sets out there. Ronin's pawn shop, Chen's noodle house, and even a history museum are collected inside.

This set is really a love letter to the Ninjago concept, setting a new standard of detail and build intricacy. And it also pairs with the other modular Lego sets in the series, connecting into one, massive street.

Lego Diagon Alley

ID code 75978
Number of pieces 5,544
Minifigures included 14

JK Rowling's boy wizard gets another entry on the list, this time at a normal Lego scale. Harry Potter Diagon Alley's 5,544 pieces combine into six modular wizarding shops: Ollivander's Wand Shop; Weasley's Wizard Wheezes; Florean Fortescue's Ice Cream Parlor; Scribbulus Writing Implements; Flourish & Blotts; and Quality Quidditch Supplies. Better yet, they're all fabulously detailed.

Windows are decorated with displays, every nook is full of color, and minor details pepper the buildings' interiors. There are plenty of optional ways to construct the set, including creating an actual alley or fitting the shops alongside other modular Lego sets to add a slice of the fictional to your dioramas.

Lego Camp Nou

Set number 10284
Number of pieces 5,509
Minifigures included 0

:As our second sports set on this list, Camp Nou - FC Barcelona makes quite the model. Coming in at 5,509 pieces, it's no small fry, but includes every possible detail of Barcelona Football Club's stadium you could think of: the stands, the press room, the player tunnels, and even a miniature team bus.

Not the only football stadium Lego has created, but definitely the largest, Camp Nou is a sight to behold.

Lego Barad-Dûr

Set number 10333
Number of pieces 5,471
Minifigures included 10

Lego Barad-Dûr immortalizes Sauron's imposing stronghold as a 33-inch-tall fortress of black bricks. Its four floors conceal a range of interactive details and gorgeous minifigs that help bring this Middle-earth monster tower to life. At the top, shining like the star on a spooky, dead Christmas tree, is the eye of Sauron, which is illuminated by a light brick.

At 18 inches wide and 12 inches deep, Barad-Dûr is most impressive for its height. Its value for money will also wow, with around 20 hours of build time needed to set this big boy up. Expect a fairly complex but satisfying build experience (with lots of similar color bricks to sort).

And should eighteen inches be too small for your tastes, you can even stack multiple Barad-Dûrs one atop the other, thanks to the modular design of the levels.

Lego Venator Republic Attack Cruiser

Set number 75367
Number of pieces 5,374
Minifigures included 2

The magnificent Lego Venator-Class Republic Attack Cruiser was the hottest thing in Lego Star Wars in 2023. Though the Venator is only a minor player in the mainline Star Wars movies, it starred in many episodes of the Clone Wars animated series, developing a cult following among fans.

A bit smaller than its original trilogy-era variant, the UCS Star Destroyer, the Venator comes in at 43 inches long, with 5,374 pieces total. A measly two minifigures come with the set - a slight disappointment to some - but the choices of Captain Rex and Admiral Yularen will please Clone Wars superfans.

Lego Avengers Tower

Set number 76269
Number of pieces 5,201
Minifigures included 31

The Lego Avengers Tower stands at a heroic 36 inches tall. Most of this height is made up of glass windows, which are a real chore to attach, but the final result is stunning. Inside the tower itself, you'll find lots of  Marvel Cinematic Universe Easter eggs. Combine this with a small army of minifigures, and you've got a wonderful bit of fan-service.

Yes, we've seen many of these minifigs before. And yes, the set is pretty pricey. But its staggering size and fabulous display value make it a worthy investment for any Marvel fan - or Lego fan.

2007 UCS Millennium Falcon

Set number 10179
Number of pieces 5,197
Minifigures included 5

The 2007 UCS Millennium Falcon set was the last word in Lego Star Wars for a full decade. When it launched it was one of the biggest sets ever made, and its still one of the largest Lego sets to this day. With just shy of 5,200 pieces, this is a long yet engaging build. The final product is a stunning display piece that's packed with detail (though it's way too big to be played with).

We're not sure we'd recommend buying one - the newer model is just as pretty and widely available, while this version can only be bought second-hand for at least three times its original price. But if you're a hardcore collector, this will be one of your holy grails.

Lego Hogwarts Express Collector's Edition

Set number 76405
Number of pieces 5,129
Minifigures included 20

There have been many brick-based renditions of the famous train from Harry Potter, but the Hogwarts Express Collector's Edition is the largest by far. Never before has Lego put so much detail into this steam engine.

While there's not much of a track to push the train around, the Hogwarts Express is surprisingly functional. Sliding doors, light bricks, windows you can see through, and snack trolleys that can comfortably move through its corridors are all part of the set. Also inside are mini set pieces from various Harry Potter films, with quote plaques and accurate minifigs to match.

Size often comes at a price, and this collector's edition is no exception. If you're on a budget, there are plenty of smaller versions of the train, each of them a worthy display piece in their own right. But if you want the ultimate Harry Potter display piece, this is a serious contender for the top spot.

Lego Ninjago City

A massive, modular building set.

Set number 70620
Number of pieces 4,867
Minifigures included 16

Lego Ninjago City is now only the third biggest set in the Ninjago line. However, it's still impressively large, and it's stuffed with minifigures, detail, and value for money. The build is long but rarely repetitive, and once this satisfying stage is over, you're left with a modular building that's just as fun to play with as it is to display.

Ninjago City is split into three floors, which can be lifted for easy access. The bottom level includes a bridge, sewer outlet, stream, fish market, house, service station, and taxi stand.

The functional sliding elevator then takes you to the second floor, where you'll find a fashion store, construction site, comic book store, crab restaurant, and ATM. At the very top is a radio tower, sushi bar, and apartment. Many of these come with moving parts and intriguing details that bring the location to life.

The Old Town 15th Anniversary

Set number 71861
Number of pieces 4851
Minifigures included 23

The Old Town 15th Anniversary is a celebration of fifteen years of the Ninjago TV series, and the newest Ninjago entry on this list. Packed with references and a huge cast of minifigs, this continues the Ninjago tradition of being both utterly gorgeous to look at, and incredible fun to play with.

That means it has the same weakness as the rest of the Ninjago line - this is a set that every kid will want to build, but which has some fine detail and fiddly parts that may fox some youngsters.

Lego Disney Castle

Set number 43222
Number of pieces 4,837
Minifigures included 8

The Lego Disney Castle is an updated version of the 2016 71040 set, and it's the largest Disney Lego set to date. This also means it's one of the highest priced Disney sets, but the size and detail on display help justify the high cost. Disney's most iconic building is enormous in brick form, with a regal gold-and-blue exterior and inner rooms filled with Easter eggs.

Some of Disney's most iconic couples make up the minifigures, and most are exclusive to this set. Princesses Tiana, Rapunzel, Cinderella, and Snow White appear with their beaus, and each is printed in delightful detail.

A spinning ballroom floor adds some neat functionality to the inside of the castle. With nods to Beauty and the Beast, Fantasia, and more found within, this is an ideal collector's item for any adult Disney fan. The castle is a staggering 80cm tall, though, so make sure you've got plenty of space to display it.

Lego Gringotts Wizarding Bank

Set number 76417
Number of pieces 4,801
Minifigures included 13

Gringotts Wizarding Bank is a huge multi-story Lego set, recreating the famous set piece from the Harry Potter universe. This is an enormous set in its own right, but it can also be combined with Diagon Alley. The top half of this set slots seamlessly into that diorama, creating an enhanced display piece.

The top half of the kit recreates the striking white exterior of the bank, as well as the tiny Magical Menagerie shop next door. Inside, a range of goblin minifigs are on hand to show Harry Potter and his disguised allies through the bank's marble interior. The level of detail here is excellent, and there's just enough room inside for play.

If you display Gringotts Wizarding Bank on its own, you can also attach the lower half of the set. This recreates the underground vaults of the bank, complete with a functional mine cart that minifigs can ride down to the bottom. The vaults are small, but they still conceal engaging surprises within.

UCS Star Destroyer

Set number 75252
Number of pieces 4,784
Minifigures included 2

You knew you'd find the Star Wars UCS Imperial Star Destroyer on this list somewhere. One of the most famously huge Lego sets ever made, this classic set perfectly depicts the terrifying, grey, wedge-shaped space warship that first captivated nerds in the opening seconds of A New Hope.

And it's a behemoth, too - more than three feet long, two feet wide, and over a foot high on its display stand, the powerfully gray UCS Star Destroyer takes up more than enough room on your table to honor its movie counterpart.

Sadly now retired from production, this set can be pretty pricey to pick up used. But, for serious Star Wars fans, it's probably worth it for the sheer scale and detail - from the independently poseable turbolaser turrets, to the massive, intricate engine outputs at the rear, to the adorable mini version of Leia Organa's Tantive IV that lets you act out Episode IV's opening chase (sorta).

Lego Mosaic Maker

Set number 40179
Number of pieces 4702
Minifigures included 0

What if you could turn a family portrait into a totally unique piece of Lego wall art? You can, thanks to the Lego Mosaic Maker kit!

This kit comes with 4,702 single-stud flat bricks in black, white, light gray, dark gray, and yellow, plus a 48 x 48 Lego baseplate. By uploading a picture online, you'll get a custom pixel image that shows you just how to lay out your studs on the baseplate to create your own pixel portrait.

Lego Ghostbusters Firehouse

Set number 75827
Number of pieces 4,634
Minifigures included 9

When there's something strange in your neighborhood… well, the gigantic Ghostbusters Firehouse Headquarters Lego set really won't help at all. But it is a lavish and spookily detailed recreation of the 1984 movie's classic fire station hangout.

At over a foot tall, this plus-sized, 4,634-piece playset starts out just nine inches wide, but opens out like a book until it's a full 18 inches across, exposing  a wild cornucopia of movie-accurate details inside, from toasters to toolboxes. It's very playable.

And the minifigures are the star of the show: original Ghostbusters Peter Venkman, Raymond Stantz, Egon Spengler, and Winston Zeddemore are all here, along with five other character minifigs, bit-figures for Slimer, and two colored ghosts. Now retired from production, this set will cost you a pretty penny to get a hold of.

Lego Lion Knights' Castle

ID code 10305
Number of pieces 4,514
Minifigures included 22

The Lego Lion Knight's Castle is inspired by a classic set from 1984, but that hasn't stopped it from being innovative and appealing to modern fans. This huge stone keep is stuffed with hidden details, vibrant minifigures, and seamless functional features.

This set stands at a regal 38cm high, and it's 44cm wide when closed. The two halves of the build are connected with clips, so they're easy to spread out and separate if you wish. However you wish to show it off, this is a commanding set piece from all angles, with as much detail on the inside as on the out.

The large number of minifigs and functional features make this an ideal set for play. However, the high price may put parents off gifting this to a younger fan. Grown builders will get plenty of satisfaction from putting this one together - and reminiscing about the Lego sets of days gone by.

Lego Notre-Dame de Paris

ID code 21061
Number of pieces 4,383
Minifigures included 0

The Lego Notre-Dame de Paris may not look like it belongs on the list of biggest Lego sets. At 33cm tall, 22cm wide, and 41cm deep, it's nowhere near the tallest or longest of Lego sets. However, it's joined the ranks thanks to the sheer number of parts included in the set.

The large part count gives the finished build an extreme level of detail. The historic building's iconic bell towers and stained glass windows are recreated with surprising accuracy. Creative use of several tiny Lego pieces means that everything from the gargoyles to the buttresses has been made buildable.

The downside of all these tiny pieces is that the process of building Notre-Dame is repetitive and surprisingly complex. We think that the final product is more than worth pushing through for. Lovers of architecture shouldn't miss this set.

Lego Tower Bridge

ID code 10214
Number of pieces  4,287
Minifigures included 0

2010's Lego Tower Bridge has been usurped by much larger sets, but it was one of the biggest sets by far when it launched. At 102cm long, 45cm high, and 26cm wide, it still takes up an imposing amount of space. Lego has shrunk one of London's most memorable structures to fit inside your home as a wonderfully detailed display piece.

This value comes at a steep price, though - and we're not just talking about how much this set costs on the second-hand market. The building process is particularly fiddly thanks to literally hundreds of 1×1 slopes that need placing, and there are plenty of ways to make mistakes when setting up this symmetrical structure. If you've got plenty of patience and disposable income, this shouldn't put you off too much.

Lego Harry Potter Hogwarts Crests

A wall filling Harry Potter art set.

ID code 31201
Number of pieces 4,249
Minifigures included 0

The Harry Potter Hogwarts Crests set is part of the Lego Art line. This kit builds one ornamental crest for each of the Hogwarts houses, and thanks to the special frame tiles the finished result is sturdy enough to mount on your wall.

Lego wall art isn't a challenging or interesting build - almost all the thousands of bricks in here the set are flat topped single studs, that you lay out on a grid like you're painting by numbers. And unfortunately, the finished artwork is pretty dull and lifeless. Only the most dedicated Potterheads should go looking for it.

Batman: The Animated Series Gotham City

ID code 76271
Number of pieces  4,210
Minifigures included 4

A relatively new set from early 2024, the Batman: The Animated Series Gotham City Lego set is a true beast of a display piece - a huge, wall-mountable tableau packing a ridiculous number of tucked-away details from DC Comics' beloved 1990s TV cartoon.

Apart from the set's overall scale and splendor, a closer look finds 15 separate detachable panels that hide brick-built versions of scenes, locations, and characters from the show, including the iconic animated versions of the Batcave, Batmobile, Batwing, and Wayne Manor. You get minifigures for the animated series' iterations of Bats, the Joker, Harley Quinn, and Catwoman, too.

Flat, wall-art sets aren't usually as expensive as the $300 this will set you back, but you can't argue with the monumental piece count, and for B:TAS superfans, we daresay it's worth it. Just make sure you've got the space!

Jim Lee Batman Lego Collection

ID code 31205
Number of pieces 4,167
Minifigures included 0

Another epic-scale, wall-hangable Lego art project, the Jim Lee Batman Collection set gives you big flat display boards, detailed instructions, and a metric butt-ton of colored stud pieces (over 4,000) with which to put together one of three portraits based on the work of legendary comic artist (and current DC Comics Chief Creative Officer) Jim Lee.

You can make the Caped Crusader himself, the Joker, or Harley Quinn using the pieces from one set - but buy two or three, and you can size up to a taller, full-frontal portrait of Bats, or a landscape shot of an intimate moment with Catwoman.

Sadly, the set's out of production - but you can pick it up on Ebay for about $175-230 right now.

Tropical Aquarium

ID code 10366
Number of pieces 4154
Minifigures included 0

The Lego Icons Tropical Aquarium is, frankly, beautiful. Each of the fish is an intricate mosaic of 'scale' pieces, while the coral is as cleverly constructed as any of the Lego flower sets. There are even clever mechanisms that allow the crab to pop in and out of its hidey hole, the treasure chest to open and close, and the big red fish to wiggle.

And while for the same price you could get an actual tropical aquarium, it takes a lot of skill to keep saltwater fish alive, not to mention a very high electricity bill. And these Lego fish have been sourced from a factory in Denmark - you won't have to worry that an unscrupulous dealer has captured them from the wild.

River Steamboat

ID code 21356
Number of pieces 4,090
Minifigures included 0

The Lego River Steamboat is a perfect balance of building experience and display piece. The three levels of its interior are packed with details, from a Technic engine block to the narrow dining cabins, to the bar with a full set of instruments for a live band.

Sadly, no live band is included, nor any Minifigs, which is about the only issue we can raise for this kit. It may be a little more reserved than most toy sets, but it has all the hidden detail and interactive element that make a great toy kit. You'll have a great - though sometimes challenging - time putting it together, and it will easily fit into a nook or onto a shelf, where it will look stunning.

Natural History Museum

ID code 10326
Number of pieces 4,014
Minifigures included 7

The Lego Natural History Museum is one of those perfect sets: it starts with an entertaining build, and ends with a gorgeous display piece that also has incredible play value for (careful) youngsters. And it fits into the Lego Modular Street range - perfect!

The combination of Victorian architecture with modern exhibits make this is a much more varied build than many architectural kit. The mellow color palette serves as a backdrop against which the brightly colored Minifigs - and many, many fine details concealed in the rooms - really pop.

There's just something very right about Lego - the toy famous for inspiring a love of art and science - recreating a Victorian Natural History Museum, a real-world 'palace of learning'.

Gustav Klimt - The Kiss

ID code 31221
Number of pieces 4,000
Minifigures included 0

Gustav Klimt - The Kiss recreates a masterwork of early 20th century painting. Gustav Klimt was one of the leading lights of the Art Nouveau movement in Vienna and painted The Kiss around 1907. With beautiful bold colors, flowing natural lines, and a sensual theme, it's an iconic work of romantic artwork.

You could buy a print of this incredibly famous painting for a fraction of the price of this Lego set - but for those who can afford it, this is an incredibly rewarding build, that lets you spend long slow hours luxuriating in the colors, shapes, and details of this wonderful art piece.

Biggest Lego sets FAQs

OK, so those are the biggest Lego sets ever made by number of bricks - but surely we can get nerdier than that? Here's a pile more trivia about the largest Lego sets out there!

What is the tallest Lego set?

The tallest Lego set ever sold is the 10307 Eiffel Tower, at 58.7 inches (149cm) tall. No surprises there. The second tallest set ever is also an Eiffel Tower set: its retired predecessor (set number 10181), which came out in 2007.

More interestingly, the third tallest Lego set, at 39.4 inches, is the 92176 NASA Apollo Saturn V rocket set - despite it having a comparatively titchy piece total of just 1,969! Size comes in more than one form, after all.

What is the longest Lego set?

The longest Lego set ever sold is the 10294 Titanic, at 53.1 inches (135cm).

In second place is the awesome - and sadly long retired - 10221 Super Star Destroyer, at 49.2 inches (125cm). Not quite the ship's estimated in-universe size- quoted in lore books as anywhere between 5 and 12 miles (8 to 19 kilometers) long - but that'd need an extraordinarily long shelf.

What is the smallest Lego set?

There have been at least two official numbered Lego sets containing only one piece, making them tied for the smallest set ever sold.

Our favorite examples are set 1115 - a single 4.5 volt lighting brick - and set 630, the Lego brick separator tool - although these days you get one of those in every set priced more than about $50, so most collectors technically now own multiple copies of Lego set 630!

What is the biggest Lego build ever created?

We've been talking about official Lego sets that are huge - but what about the largest actual Lego model built? Well, it's almost impossible to be sure, because avid brick fans are constantly creating enormous new projects that beggar belief with their sheer scale, detail, and in built mechanisms.

The video above, by YouTuber Astro Bricks, profiles some of the previous record holding builds - from a 112 foot long Lego suspension bridge to a 250,000 brick Woolly Mammoth. But we can go bigger.

As shown in Popular Science's video interview above, in 2013 Lego Master Builder Eric Barsegi built a life size Lego X-Wing starfighter out of - wait for it - 5.3 million bricks, that weighed 46,000 pounds.

How long does it take to build the biggest Lego sets?

On average, building a Lego set takes most people around 20 seconds per piece. That calculation is based on our own experience and collating a few different estimates online. That works out to around 65 hours' build time for the Lego World Map (the biggest Lego set ever released).

With just one person, working at that average speed, it'd take 1,227 days (nearly three and a half years) to complete the 5.3 million brick X-Wing above - the biggest overall Lego build we know of. However, in reality the time taken to build each set can vary wildly depending on which set it is, how experienced the builder is, and which method of building you choose.

If you're a master builder or just a beginner, you'll find a warm welcome in the Wargamer Discord community. And make sure you sign up to the Wargamer newsletter to get our best stories each week.

title: World Order board game review: Vying for Greatness
content:
Our Verdict

World Order is a world politics board game that feels grand and sweeping, while keeping its turns tight. It's a strong design with a lot of good stuff going on under the hood.

Pros
  • Plenty of depth, but surprisingly approachable
  • Tense, reactive gameplay
  • Great asymmetric factions
  • Gameplay closely fits the theme
Cons
  • Sprawls across the table
  • Lengthy playtime
  • Politics fans might want more player interaction

Designed to simulate the interactions between world superpowers in the year 2010, in World Order you must lead one of China, Russia, the USA, or the EU to victory on the world stage. A world power's work is never done. Over the course of six rounds you'll beaver away allying with and investing in countries, managing your natural, man-made, and political resources, constructing military bases and moving armies, all in service of putting little colored cubes onto a very familiar map and making your victory point tracker travel the furthest.

A complex game then, you might assume, and you wouldn't be wrong. But while World Order certainly looks daunting, and it's rather a table hog, it's actually much simpler than Hegemonic's last board game slash political education tool, Hegemony, and surprisingly easy to get to grips with.

Certainly, there are a lot of systems to learn here, and it takes a good deal of strategy to play this game well. But once you've grasped the core rules, World Order's advantage is that each turn is relatively short and simple. You usually play one card, take one action, and say go. This is still a lengthy game, one you schedule in for half a day rather than pull off the shelf when you've got a few free hours, but there's very little down time between turns, which helps to keep the whole table engaged.

At the beating heart of World Order is a card system, which is its action economy, and a resource control game, which is your main objective. You start with a deck of cards that you'll draw from to determine your possible moves each round. Each (typically) has one of eight different actions you can take: improve relations, trade, engage, move, build a base, produce resources, get a growth card, or invest.

You'll only play one card each turn, and there are four turns each round. With six rounds in the game total, that means each player only takes 24 actions in an entire game of World Order. This makes every turn feel important, and you'll strive to reach your goals as efficiently as possible, desperate not to waste a single move. However, you won't have every action available to you on every round, forcing you to make hard choices - like foregoing points now to set yourself up for future success.

Every action type has its place. You need to trade to get resources or money, improve relations to gain allied countries that make other actions easier (or possible), move armies around the board to keep control over the regions you have a vested interest in, and gain development cards to gain points and more flexible powers.

But your ultimate goal (i.e. the biggest source of points) is to have the most influence in seven different regions, which means you need to build bases or invest in your allied countries, or else engage in the region with your political power.

This territory-control aspect is where most of World Order's tension comes from. It's a zero-sum game. It's not good enough having a little influence across the whole Earth - you need to win particular regions. To do this, you have to watch your opponents carefully, figure out what they're up to, and decide where you're going to be able to compete and where it just isn't worth the battle.

This feeling of responding to others actions applies to World Order's military system too. There is no combat, instead each superpower has particular regions they're interested in. If your rivals have more armies in those regions than you (the EU and USA don't count each other as enemies for this) then you'll bleed points at the end of each round. This means, instead of a heated war where armies win or lose conflicts, you have a constantly growing military build-up, a sort of Cold War situation, with neither side firing a shot.

This system works, feels suitably thematic, and allows your opponents' actions to shape your own, but it's not super dynamic. Either you have the most military in a region, someone else does, or you're in deadlock. I could seldom see any reason to ever deescalate once tanks were committed to a region, for instance.

World Order features the best kind of asymmetry, where you only have to learn one set of mechanics but each faction still feels dramatically different to play. Each power produces different amounts of each resource, has its own starting deck, its own unique scoring incentives, two special once-per-game ability cards, and begins the game with different allies and starting influence. The differences between players are more subtle than a game like Root (or Hegemony for that matter) but in practice this usually works out better. The factions feel suitably different without massively extending 'The Teach'.

I want to talk a little more about the influence system, because it's so instrumental to the game and it has some interesting nuances. Each region has temporary and permanent influence slots, and, space permitting, you choose which type you want to add whenever you gain influence.

But while temporary influence gives you more victory points in the short term, it can be dislodged by your opponents. When there's no room left, a new temporary influence cube pushes the others one space to the left, which means whoever placed theirs first gets shoved off. An additional complexity: regions won't score in one of the two scoring periods (at the end and half-way through) unless all their permanent influence squares are filled up.

From my experience, this turns the first half of the game into a land-grab, with each player striving to scoop up as many permanent influence spots as possible, and also ensure their regions score come turn three. The latter half then becomes a cat-and-mouse game, where players want to wait and see, only committing influence to the regions they're in contention for when they're sure it won't just be removed again. Such a simple system, but it creates really fun shifts in the strategy.

Another interesting mechanic in World Order is the game's light deck-building element. You draw six action cards in a round and use four, and the ones left in your hand then give you resources (usually cash, political power, or tanks) and research to buy new cards.

This adds a particularly heartwrenching dilemma, as you have to decide between taking the best actions in the round, or preserving cards to buy new ones for later. Honestly, I found this a little paralyzing, and so mostly focused on making the best choices in the moment, just keeping the idea of saving some research in the back of my mind, rather than planning out what I wanted to buy ahead of schedule.

I think this may actually be the intended approach, because the deck-building in World Order is relatively minor. Compared to a somewhat similar game, Dune Imperium, you cycle through your cards less often, and you only have five opportunities to buy more. It's perfectly possible in fact, that you won't be able to buy anything every round. Indeed, in one game, playing China, I missed over half of the opportunities to pick up new cards, but still managed to take second place.

Not that the new cards aren't worthwhile. Strong cards let you take multiple actions at once, or give a minor effect while letting you play a second card. Others might give you a slightly superior version of a regular action or let you reset temporary influence at the same time, upsetting the applecart, as a different player now stands to have their influence pushed out.

When teaching World Order to less experienced gamers, I found the real-life theme helped quite a lot. While action cards with names like Assign New Diplomats and Minimize Bureaucracy aren't going to thrill anyone's pants off, the fact that World Order tries to be a political simulation, aligning with real life as closely as possible, makes it feel easier to learn.

This doesn't just apply to little particulars like the US being unable to cosy up with North Korea (it's 2010, not 2026), it also works when applied to each power's overall strategy. Russia wants to go big on military, China wants to sell consumer goods to the world and get rich, the EU wants to make friends, and the US wants to be a global superpower and do everything at once, requiring careful decision-making to avoid spreading itself too thin.

There were even bits of moment-to-moment gameplay where I found the - is it ludonarrative harmony? - very satisfying. For instance, while Russia was causing problems for me with its military posturing, I as the EU still had to buy tons of fuel from them. That's Realpolitik, baby!

There is one place where the theme doesn't really match the experience. For a game about politics, there's no deal-making to be done (any trades are forced) and while you're always responding to others' actions, there's practically no direct interaction between players. I think adding this in would've just bogged the game down, but it's worth mentioning, as this could be an expectation mismatch for a potential player.

From what I've experienced, World Order works well at different play counts - from two to four. While probably best with four, it has an extremely easy-to-run automata system representing the actions of any absent powers. This adds an element of randomness. You can also see what these NPCs are going to do ahead of time, creating a slightly different dynamic as you prepare for their moves.

The production value of World Order is top notch. I love its chunky wooden tanks, and I love that your resource count is tracked by moving wooden resource symbols along a track. A lesser game would've done this with big piles of different token types. I'm not a fan of the tiny country cards - little, hard-to-shuffle decks are the bane of my existence - but otherwise, it gets a gold star.

You'll need a large table though. While World Order doesn't have unnecessary components, those it does have are pretty large, and between a huge central map, individual player boards, and room required all over for various cards, the game takes up a ton of space. It packs away very neatly and intuitively though, something I always appreciate.

Overall, designers Vangelis Bagiartakis and Varnavas Timotheou have skillfully made a game that sticks in your head long after you're done playing. Its many systems bely a relatively simple core gameplay loop, and there's plenty of replay value here as you try out different factions and strategies. I think this is a really clever game, and it's the sort of title that some people will find really fun to master.

Even if that's not you, if you have any interest in this theme and don't mind a longer strategy board game, I heartily recommend giving World Order a whirl.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: XCOM The Miniatures Game Wave 1 Aliens and Operatives
content:
Thanks to Modiphius for providing these models for review.

When Modiphius announced XCOM: The Miniatures Game, I was more than a little bit excited. As no stranger to the video games or Modiphius' previous resin and plastic offerings, I wasted no time in jumping on a call with Chris Birch, Modiphius' CEO, and interviewed them about their new project. Suitably hyped, I got cracking on their first wave of releases. Said wave covers the first Operatives set - consisting of 6 XCOM Operatives, and the first Alien wave, which includes 3 Sectoids, 1 Sectoid Commander, 3 Thin Men, and 1 Outsider. I was sent the resin versions, though plastic versions of the same sculpts are also going to be available.

Details

XCOM Operatives on sprue. Credit: SRM

I started with the Operatives, as they're the folks I've spent hundreds of hours sending to their deaths in the video games. The details are as crisp and clean as I'd expect from Modiphius. The guns even have undercuts at the ends of their barrels so you don't need to drill them out. Cleanup was fairly minor; some flashing around the boots, the odd mold line on the gun, and no huge, obvious mold lines in inopportune places. The Sniper had some light mold slipping along the legs but nothing a knife couldn't fix. The faces are expressive and a little cartoony - honestly, the whole set has a cartoony look very much in line with the modern Firaxis-developed XCOM games. The weapons are chunky, the armor is blocky, and there aren't any overdone details that will make painting a pain. In short, these models are clean and simple, but I mean that in a positive way - excessive detail and sharp detail are not the same thing. The only thing I don't really love are the sculpted eyebrows, which can look a little too cartoony on models this scale.

XCOM Wave 1 Aliens on sprue. Credit: SRM

The aliens might appear simpler at first glance (after all, a Sectoid is just a classic "Roswell grey" alien) but have some sharp detail too. The folds in the Thin Men's suits are crisp, the musculature on the aliens is well-defined with some creepy veins around the Sectoid Commander's brain, while the Outsider's armor and the crew's weapons all have clean, sharp edges to them. These guys involved a bit more cleanup than the Operatives, with more flashing and mold lines to deal with, but nothing too egregious.

If you're used to Modiphius' models, you might have been expecting sculpted scenic bases. These guys have simple plastic 30mm bases, just a smidge shorter than Games Workshop's. I was missing one, so I filled in with a 32mm base from my bits box. Given the variety of locales an average XCOM campaign can take you, I don't mind getting to choose for myself how to base these guys, though it wouldn't shock me if Modiphius made base toppers in the future for this like they have for Fallout.

Assembly

The preview copies we got didn't have instructions, but it wasn't a big deal in this case. The models rarely consist of more than 3 or 4 parts, and each resin sprue is stamped with a number that makes it easy to tell what goes with what. Sprues MXU 005A and MXU 005B are one model, MXU 001A and MXU 001B are another, and so on. There was a little more confusion on the alien side, but when in doubt, just look at the product photos and see how they want to go together. Most pieces fit with a pretty simple peg and divot that has a tiny bit of wiggle room. Being resin, there's often a bit of warping or bending that makes a few fits kind of wonky. Most cases where I had two arms holding a gun, I had to cut at least some of their guiding pegs to better fit the arms together. The joins on the Operatives are very well hidden, largely lining up with armor plates and the like. The Sectoids aren't quite so lucky, being so organic, but the other aliens have well hidden joins too. Even with a few minutes given to base decor and locating an extra base for the Outsider, it took me like an hour and a half to build both sets.

XCOM Operatives WIP. Credit: SRM

My only real complaint here is that there's no variety or options should you end up with more than one of these groups of Operators. You can swap the arms on some of them pretty readily if you wanted to change things up, but aside from the sniper, all of their heads are integrated with their bodies. It would have been nice to have head options, just for variety's sake. I understand that more models will come in the future which will likely have some of the other heads, helmets, and hairstyles we've seen in the games, but I would have liked a couple options in this initial offering. XCOM Operatives are very much "your dudes" in the video games, and I would have liked to see that better reflected here.

XCOM Aliens wave 1 WIP. Credit: SRM

By their nature, the aliens of this wave are much more diverse. The Sectoids and Sectoid Commander are fiddly, with thin arms and small contact points. The one on all fours was especially tricky, and I could never line up the Commander's arms quite right. In a few cases I had to just cut off the guiding pegs to stick the limbs on, and I was even using fresh superglue. The Thin Men have larger pieces which fit together more easily, though I had to brace the long outstretched gun arm. There was some confusion on the crouching pair's weapon arms, but dry fitting quickly made it clear which gun went with which guy. Lastly, the Outsider was chunky enough that he took no effort at all.

Painting

As I've mentioned in my previous Fallout painting articles, I treat painting models from a property like this the same way I'd approach a historical miniature. I gather reference material from places like the XCOM wiki (get your adblockers ready, it's a Fandom page) and then base my schemes on those. Most screenshots out there are low-resolution given the game's age and its more niche fandom, but it's hardly a big ask to open up XCOM: Enemy Unknown and start nabbing screenshots of your own, or crawling around on Steam for recent shots from the community. It was helpful to also have a tab with the studio paint jobs up too, but they differ from the game models in a few ways here and there.

XCOM Wave 1 Aliens. Credit: SRM

The aliens were first, as I figured they'd be easy to knock out given their simpler details and textures. I painted all of the alien weapons in Grey Seer and Thamar Black, with highlights of Ulthuan Grey and Dawnstone respectively. They have kind of a 2010s Apple store aesthetic, and I wanted to distinguish their alien materials from human ones by using non-metallic colors. For the green of the plasma, I'd pick that out in Caliban Green then highlight with Warboss Green and Skarsnik Green.

XCOM Sectoids. Credit: SRM

The Sectoids seemed most straightforward, so I started there. I primed them with Mechanicus Standard Grey, and washed them with thinned Drakenhof Nightshade, plus some thinned Gal Vorbak Red in some deep muscles for color variation. The Sectoid Commander got a Carroburg Crimson wash on his top half as well, and they all got some Carroburg Crimson around the eyes. I built the grey of the skin back up with the base color, and did a two stage highlight, gradually adding more Fenrisian Grey to it to give them their blue-grey skintone.

XCOM Sectoid Commander. Credit: SRM

For the Sectoid Commander, I added a little Emperor's Children to that mix to highlight his veins and brain. I picked out the eyes in Gal Vorbak Red, with a little black mixed in for the pupils. For their sickly yellow glow, I tried a Cassandora Yellow wash then some thinned Yriel Yellow paint, but wasn't crazy with the look. It got the point across, but were I to paint more Sectoids in the future I'd probably try something else.

XCOM Thin Men. Credit: SRM

I primed the Thin Men with Chaos Black primer, since they're just creepy dudes in dark suits. A blend of Thamar Black and Dark Reaper made for the first highlight, and pure Dark Reaper for the second. Their skin was Rakarth Flesh, washed with Seraphim Sepia and then Athonian Camoshade around the visible scales on their necks and wrists. They have kind of a sickly look in the game, and I think that got there. I reestablished the base color, leaving shades in the recesses, and highlighted their chins, cheekbones, eyebrows and noses with Pallid Wych Flesh. I then picked their scales out with Caliban Green and highlighted those with a mix of Caliban Green and Grey Seer, since those colors were still wet on my palette. Any lighter green will probably do. Their ties were just Wazdakka Red with Wild Rider Red highlights, and their buttons and glasses were picked out in Retributor Armour. I highlighted their hair with Eshin Grey and their shoes with Skavenblight Dinge and Stormvermin Fur on their sharpest points, just to give them a sharp, warm look.

XCOM Outsider. Credit: SRM

The Outsider was the biggest challenge to figure out. While the studio paint job is lovely, finding reference photos from the games was much harder. For one, they're less prevalent than the other aliens, only showing up on UFO crashes, so there aren't as many images out there. For two, they're a messy ball of polygons around a crystal, and clean images of them are in short supply. I turned to the starting point of any would-be ROMhacker or 2000s sprite-based webcomic creator, Spriter's Resource, which had a clear model of an Outsider, plus a few other aliens and items from the game. After that, it became pretty clear which panels were brown and which were grey, and I was able to pick them out in Gorthor Brown and Corvus Black, respectively. I washed the whole thing with Agrax Earthshade, reestablished the base colors, and highlighted the brown with Rakarth Flesh and black with Mechanicus Standard Grey. He's got way more edges than anything else in the alien crew, so was a little tedious to paint, but it made figuring out what colors go where pretty simple.

XCOM Outsider. Credit: SRM

The crystal he's built around was just Averland Sunset, washed Cassandora Yellow, and highlighted with Yriel Yellow.

XCOM Operatives. Credit: SRM

For the Operatives, I wanted to paint them like their standard appearance in the game, which is a brown, tan, and green uniform. I started with Hinox Brown primer (the equivalent of Citadel's Rhinox Hide) and worked my way up from there. I put down base coats of Castellan Green for their BDUs, Tallarn Sand for the tan parts of their armor and weapons, Corvus Black for the dark fabric straps and pads on their armor, Evil Sunz Scarlet for the red cloth on the rifle magazines, lenses on scopes, and shotgun shells, and Loren Forest for the grenades, while leaving the boots in their primer brown. I united all of these with a wash of Athonian Camoshade, reestablished their base colors while leaving shades in the recesses, and gave them a quick round of highlights - Loren Forest for the green, Karak Stone for the tan, Mechanicus Standard Grey for the black, Wild Rider Red for the reds, and Gorthor Brown for the dark brown boots. I gave them a diverse set of skintones using (dark to light) Catachan Flesh, Bloodreaver Flesh, Knight-Questor Flesh, Cadian Fleshtone, and Kislev Flesh. I would base one of those colors, wash with Reikland Fleshshade, establish that base and blend in a little of the next color in line. Eyes were just black with white in the corners. Lastly, I painted the metallics, mostly because I don't like painting metallics. These were just Leadbelcher with Nuln Oil wash, highlighted with Pro Acryl Silver (Stormhost Silver equivalent).

XCOM Sniper Operative. Credit: SRM

Every Operative has a tiny square on their collar where you can paint a flag, representing their home country and the international, collaborative nature of the XCOM project. I'm sure someone out there makes tiny enough decals to pop here, but I just painted a few by hand. My recommendation would be to choose simpler flags, or abstract ones that are more complicated. After all, it's a surface only marginally larger than a grain of rice, so don't try to get all 50 stars if you're painting an American flag or something similarly detailed. I'd also go for more saturated colors here than on your base models just to make them stand out more.

XCOM Support Operatives. Credit: SRM

I united all of the models with a lush forest basing scheme, first for color contrast and second because it can represent so many places in the world. I used a few leftover basing bits from Epic Basing that I'd gotten in one swag bag or another, plus the single Medikit that came on the sprue of one of the Support Operatives, with the same red and white recipes as on the XCOM Operatives and the Alien weapons. The ground was just Stirland Mud texture paint, washed Agrax Earthshade and drybrushed with Steel Legion Drab and Karak Stone. I added tufts from Army Painter and Woodland Scenics clump foliage for some denser grown and called it a day.

Final Thoughts, Parting Shots, and What Have You

XCOM Assault Operatives. Credit: SRM

Working with these models was a generally pleasant experience. Building them could be a bit finnicky, as their cartoony, video game designs were probably never meant to exist in the physical world and likely weren't made with considerations towards that. The sculptors at Modiphius did a great job translating those designs to physical miniatures, and holding these little guys who've only existed on my screen for over a decade was a delight. This is a solid start for the XCOM range, though I don't feel it'll hit its full potential until we start seeing the multi-part plastic kits they've mentioned. This may be a humble beginning, but it's a promising one.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: [40k] Ruleshammer 11th Edition: Article Updates #3 (August FAQs)
content:
Welcome back to Ruleshammer! In this series we take a detailed look at the rules of key games; Warhammer 40k in particular and, right now, in specific. This week I’m covering more reader questions and looking at what’s changed with the August Update!

Shooting Phase

When is Damage modified to 0?

Q: My unit has access to a rule that changes the Damage characteristic of an incoming attack to 0. When such an attack is allocated to a model in that unit, is the Damage changed before or after save rolls?

A: After.

This FAQ follows a change in the way allocation works in 11th edition compared to previous editions. In 11th, while the order of allocation groups is decided before saves, the “thing” actually allocated to specific models is essentially a save roll, and they are allocated to the group from lowest to highest. This all occurs in Step 4 Inflict Damage 05.04.

The opposing player resolves the following sequence for each save roll, working from lowest result(s) to highest result(s),...

Another element of this scenario worth noting here, though, is that abilities that reduce attacks to 0 damage in 11th got a small buff due to how modifiers work in the new edition.

Note that rules that modify a characteristic in this step to a new value of ‘0’, ‘-’ or ‘*’ cannot be modified by other rules (in such cases, skip steps 2-5).

In 10th edition, whilst modifying damage to 0 did still happen before other modifiers it did not block further modification; weapons such as MELTA 2 previously could improve an attack reduced to 0 damage back up to 2. In 11th edition, that is no longer the case.

Critical Hits on X+ with or within Snap Shooting

The return of snap shooting as a concept in 11th has allowed GW to actually create a slight compromise to what these two FAQs now address.

Q: My attack has a rule that means it results in a critical hit on a hit roll of 4+, and I would otherwise need a 5+ to hit. Does a 4+ hit?

A: Yes, except when snap shooting: when snap shooting, each attack only hits on a roll of 6.

Q: My attack has a rule that means it results in a critical hit on a hit roll of 4+. Does this work when snap shooting?

A: Unless otherwise stated, no: when snap shooting, each attack only hits on a roll of 6.

In the past these abilities have tended to need a successful hit on the die i.e. if a 5+ was needed to hit then you needed a 5+ even with this ability, but that’s largely seemed to be because they specifically did not want these abilities to result in 4+ shooting when using Overwatch. Now that Overwatch has its own unique shooting rule in Snap Shooting, it’s allowed them to use that as an exclusion. So now Critical Hits on 4+ will always be Critical Hits on 4+ except when firing Overwatch.

Visibility Checks When Toeing Into Terrain

This is another one of those edge cases I’ve gotten the most questions about, and for many new players it can be confusing when “True Line of Sight” applies or doesn’t.

Follow this link for more Ruleshammer on Terrain. 

Charge Phase

Take to the Skies and Charges

These two FAQs are some of the more frustrating ones, as the timing of Take to The Skies just flatly contradicts the answer we’re given here.

Q: When do the effects of a FLYING unit taking to the skies apply?

A: When that unit is selected to make a normal/advance/fall-back/charge move. Note that for an advance/charge move, this means you must declare that a unit will take to the skies before rolling for that advance/charge move.

and

Q: How do modifiers to the charge roll (or to the maximum distance of the charge move, such as Take to the Skies) affect the selection of charge targets?

A: A charging unit may only select charge targets that are within the maximum distance of their charge roll, including any modifiers. If such a modifier occurs after selecting a charge target and causes that charge target to no longer be within the maximum distance, the charging unit would then select new targets (Target No Longer Eligible Or Viable, 04.03.03). Example: A unit's charge roll is 7", and that unit has a datasheet ability which adds 1 to charge rolls: that charge's maximum distance is 8", so you can select charge targets within 8". Example: A FLYING unit chooses to take to the skies and rolls a charge roll of 9"; that charge's maximum distance is 7" (9" minus the 2" from taking to the skies), so you can select charge targets within 7".

The intended ruling of these FAQs is clear: We have to decide to Take to the Skies BEFORE rolling advance or charge rolls. However, my complaint here is that the trigger in the Take to the Skies rules is making a charge move.

Each time a FLYING unit is selected to make a normal, advance, fall-back or charge move,

And you make Charge Moves after rolling the charge distance; that happens when you declare a charge. I’d really like to see this rule updated in the future to use that moment instead, swap it to “declare a charge” and the rule and FAQ align without issue.

Follow this link for more Ruleshammer on the Charge Phase.

Fight Phase

Fight on Death Models

This FAQ confirms something I’ve been meaning to make a diagram for for a while: Fight On Death models can block movement during the fight phase until they fight and are removed.

Q: Fight On Death (05.04.05) requires models awaiting such an ability to stay on the battlefield until their unit has attacked (or until the end of the phase). How do these models function while this is the case?

A: Models awaiting a Fight On Death ability are still present on the battlefield for all rules purposes. This includes (but is not limited to) the following regarding such models: They can be measured to by friendly/enemy abilities. They can be considered visible to friendly/enemy models where relevant. They can use their datasheet abilities. They can be targeted by stratagems. Enemy units can still be engaged with them (which may restrict the opposing player's consolidation/pile-In moves made as part of an overrun fight).

It’s entirely possible to not even be eligible to make an Overrun Fight in this situation.

Consolidation Move Changes

12.08 - Consolidation Move, After Moving Section, Ongoing Consolidation

Change to: Each model that started this move engaged with an enemy unit must still be engaged with that enemy unit. If one or more enemy units engaged with your unit have not been selected to fight this phase, your opponent must select each of those units, one at a time; when each is selected, it becomes eligible to fight and is selected to fight

This FAQ closes one of the edge cases we had from the Consolidation step. It was entirely possible to engage new units with an ongoing consolidation who hadn’t been eligible to fight earlier in the phase. and were now arguably still unable to fight. as the fight step was over and only Engaging Consolidation had a specific part that enabled newly engaged units to fight. This addition specifically allows those newly engaged units to fight after this consolidation move is resolved, before resolving any others.

Follow this link for more Ruleshammer on the Fight Phase.

Transports

New Disembark Moves

This update adds two new Disembark Moves to the roster, Assault Disembark Moves and Shock Disembark moves! These two moves and their associated FAQ resolve an issue with the current disembark move that I didn’t even notice. If your model has an ability such as the Devilfish’s Rapid Deployment, it didn’t have a valid Disembark move type.

Rapid Deployment: Units can disembark from this TRANSPORT after it has Advanced. Units that do so count as having made a Normal move that phase, and cannot declare a charge in the same turn, but can otherwise act normally in the remainder of the turn.

Or the Land Raiders’ Assault Ramp ability.

Assault Ramp: Each time a unit disembarks from this model after it has made a Normal move, that unit is still eligible to declare a charge this turn.

This also did not previously have a valid disembark move type to choose other than Combat Disembark; Rapid Disembark required the transport to have made a normal or ingress move, while Tactical Disembark required a transport to have remained stationary, meaning these abilities required you to make hazard rolls and the unit became battle-shocked. That's something the new Disembark moves show was clearly not intended.

There is however one small issue with the new moves that I hope is addressed quickly in the app:

The new Shock Disembark’s after moving section doesn’t really seem to make sense; in fact it appears to be the wording added to the Consolidation rules for Ongoing Consolidations (see above). I strongly suspect that this section should actually read:

"AFTER MOVING: Until the end of the turn your unit is not eligible to declare a charge."

As of right now, that section doesn’t make much sense; a unit embarked within a transport can’t start their disembark move engaged with anything, as it’s not on the battlefield. Fortunately the abilities themselves do preclude making a charge, so we can be pretty confident on the RAI here.

Abilities in Transports

Q: Do a unit's abilities continue to function while they are embarked within a TRANSPORT?

A: Yes, within the restrictions specified by the ability itself. Embarked units are Not On The Battlefield (01.02.04), so any ability requiring visibility or measurement to another unit will fail. Example: Azrael is attached to an Intercessor Squad unit and embarked within a TRANSPORT, and that TRANSPORT is making a shooting attack using the Firing Deck ability. While Azrael's Supreme Grand Master ability is still technically active, it will have no effect, as the requirements of the ability are not met (the ability affects 'weapons equipped by models' in Azrael's unit, and for the purposes of Firing Deck, the TRANSPORT itself is equipped with those weapons instead).

This FAQ confirms that weapons modified by an ability of an embarked unit don’t work when the weapon is then equipped by the transport. Why they couldn’t have in some way avoided this strange situation where transports ignore transitive properties and instead get versions of the weapons different to the ones their embarked unit is carrying, I’m not sure, but at least we know the intended ruling for this now.

Other New FAQs and Errata

Here’s a summary of other FAQs and Errata added in the August 2026 Update that are fairly self explanatory.

FAQs

Q: Can I use the Insane Bravery stratagem on a battle-shocked unit?

A: No, as a unit's controlling player cannot target that unit with stratagems (01.07).

Q: If a rule refers to an 'objective marker', does this mean an 'objective'?

A: Yes (excluding rules in the Core Rules).

Q: If both players have units with the Scouts ability, do they alternate resolving scout moves?

A: Yes, players alternate resolving any pre-battle rules units from their army may have, starting with the player who will take the first turn.

Q: When checking line of sight from one model to another, is this drawn between the bases of those models, or between any part of them?

A: Line of sight is drawn from any part of the observing model to any part of the model being observed.

Q: Units have all the keywords of all their models, and attached units have all the keywords of all of their component units. How are destroyed models taken into account for these purposes?

A: These statements are only true so long as the models possessing those keywords remain part of the unit; destroyed models do not contribute their keywords to their prior unit. Example: The Aspiring Sorcerer model in a unit of Rubric Marines is destroyed; as none of the remaining models in the unit possess the PSYKER keyword, that unit is no longer a PSYKER unit.

Errata

01.02.06 A unit must be split into two units, each containing as equal a number of models as possible (when splitting a unit in this way, make a note of which models form each of the two new units). If a rule states a specific starting strength of the split units, but this is not possible based on the number of models in the unit being split (e.g. due to attached Leader/Support models), split the unit as stated above.

24.08 Deadly Demise.

Change to: Each time a model with this ability is destroyed, after the … each unit within 6").

22.03.01 Psychic Abilities with a Psychic Level.

When using psychic abilities with a psychic level, a PSYKER unit cannot use the same psychic ability more than once per phase.
