title: Trench Crusade Warband Focus: Papal States Intervention Force
content:
Welcome everyone to another Trench Crusade Warband focus! This time we’re looking into the Papal States Intervention Force. When the Supreme Pontiff of Rome wants something done, they send in this squad. Let’s take a look at why this force is one to be reckoned with. 

The Lore

Image: Beezer

Operating under the command of the Supreme Pontiff of Rome, these warriors are sent to the front lines on vital missions, from eliminating key leaders to recovering important artifacts of particular spiritual significance. 

The force is small but includes some of the most elite soldiers available, led by warrior monks and priests selected by the Pope themself. Backing up these soldiers is an arsenal of specialized equipment that no one else has access to.

The Variant

Before we get into things, let’s quickly break down the Variant’s rules: 

  • Far from Home: You cannot include Trench Moles.
  • Lector: You do not have to include a Lieutenant in your warband, but you must include a Trench Cleric, and this Cleric gains the Leader keyword, as well as the Arise and be Healed! ability: 
  • Arise and be Healed!: After a successful Risky Roll, the Cleric may pick another unit within 3” (including themselves). That unit stands up if Downed and can remove up to D3 Blood Markers and/or Infection Markers. 
  • Specialist Force: This rule is what makes this Variant so unique. Essentially, when you start a campaign, or even a one-off, you start off with 200 fewer Ducats than usual (so 500 Ducats for a first campaign game). However, you start off with 11 Glory (adjusting for one-offs or late campaign joining) to compensate.
  • Supreme Blessing: You must give the Supreme Pontiff’s Crucifix to one model at warband creation, at no extra cost. If you lose it, you gotta buy another. 
  • Swiss Guard: Your Lieutenant and up to 4 other models gain the Negate Fear Keyword for no additional cost (modeling these models with cool hats is optional, but recommended)

Whilst the amount of changes may be smaller than most variants, the impact of each individual change is far-reaching. The massive change to your warband construction is how you spend your Glory. Do you focus on Glory Items or Mercenaries? Glory Items can stay around and provide longer-term value when on your Elites, but Mercenaries pad out your unit count. Each has their pros and cons, and you’ll need experience to get a feel for this new way to build lists. Even when it comes to playing a game, this change significantly affects how you approach the scenario. Do you want to go for more Glory? How do you want to protect your Mercenaries, as the loss of a Merc is a big dent in your Glory economy?

Unique Battlekit

Supreme Pontiff’s Crucifix - 3 Glory - Limit: 1

A very simple but effective piece of Equipment, where the bearer’s activation does not immediately end if they fail a Risky Success Roll. This is such a great piece of Equipment for your Lector, who has two abilities that require a Risky Success Roll, on top of their Dash Action. Throw a Med-Kit on them too, or anything else that requires a Risky Success Roll, and you have a unit that can consistently contribute without fear of needing to map out their activation.

Key Units

Lector

Marco Veneziano. Image: Beezer

The Lector (aka, a Trench Cleric) will be your key piece in your warband, not only because it could potentially replace your Lieutenant, but also because their reliability can skyrocket, as they will most likely be the bearer of the Supreme Pontiff’s Crucifix. Not having to worry about the consequences of failing Dashes or using Arise and Be Healed! will ensure that the Lector gets to at least try and succeed at every ability they have (let’s not forget, God Is with Us also requires a Risky Success Roll) 

Recommend Starting Loadout: 

  • Automatic Pistol / Automatic Rifle / Submachine Gun
  • Supreme Pontiff’s Crucifix

Witchburner

Witchburner General. Credit: SRM

Now I know that you’re wondering why a Mercenary is a key unit for this Warband, but remember that Papal States gets easy access to Mercenaries thanks to a large amount of Glory upfront, and you need to bump up your unit count in the early game. 

With that in mind, the Witchburner is a great unit to take early. As they have the Elite keyword, you can start to generate Experience and gain skills for them early, really helping them contribute beyond their initial skillset. 

The Witchburner is slow to get up the board, but their worth comes from their Divine Judgment ability, which ignores Line of Sight and allowing you to dish out Blood Markers to the units that you want to. With a healthy 24” range that is not hindered by Cover or Long-Range penalties, it ensures the Witchburner contributes despite them needing to slowly swagger up the board. 

Communicant Anti-Tank Hunter

Communicant Anti-Tank Hunter. Credit: SRM

A staple in almost every list at some point, the Communicant Anti-Tank Hunter gives you amazing early game pressure, where your enemies' key long-range units need to be extra careful. Usually, an enemy Artillery Witch has relative freedom in early campaign games, as long-range weaponry is a little more sparse. However, with a Papal States force with a Communicant Anti-Tank Hunter, the Artillery Witch has to be very careful with their positioning; otherwise it goes bye-bye. 

Other Faithful factions can only dream of having such early game Armour Ignoring pressure. 

The List

Supreme Pwntiff

Faction: Papal States Intervention Force

Rating: 500 Ducats | 14 Glory

Patron: None

## Elites ##

Lector - 110D | 3G

Battlekit: Automatic Pistol, Medi-Kit, Supreme Pontiff ’s Crucifix, Standard Armour, Trench Shield

Sniper Priest - 76D

Battlekit: Automatic Pistol, Pistol

Witchburner - 5G

Battlekit: Gavel of Justice, Combat Helmet, Reinforced Armour

## Troops ##

Yeoman - 52D

Battlekit: Musical Instrument, Frag Grenades

Mechanized Heavy Infantry - 120D

Battlekit: Heavy Shotgun, Reinforced Armour, Satchel Charge

Combat Engineer - 105D

Battlekit: Shotgun, Shovel, Engineer Body Armour, Satchel Charge

Yeoman - 37D

Battlekit: Frag Grenades

## Mercenaries ##

Communicant Anti-Tank Hunter - 6G

Battlekit: Anti-Materiel Rifle, Trench Club, Trench Club, Combat Helmet

So, with this list, the most difficult aspect was keeping my Ducat cost down by including only the most vital aspects. With a 500 Ducat limit, you really have to stick to just the core aspects of New Antioch: a MHI and Combat Engineer with Satchel Charges, a cheap Yeoman (who will get Flamethrowers asap), and a cheap but effective Sniper Priest. Pistols and Automatic Pistols help ensure your models contribute in range and melee without pinching the purse too much. Grenades are on the cheap Yeoman to not only hold objectives, but put on Blood Markers for cheap. 

The Lector, however, is packed with more equipment. They, of course, take the Crucifix, and I added on a med-kit, so they can heal units twice without worrying about failing a Risky roll. 

The big downside here is the complete lack of a Tough model, so if things go well, it’s good to grab a Lieutenant to ensure you at least have some kind of Tough in the list and can be more aggressive. 

Final Thoughts

The Papal States play a completely different, but very fun game when it comes to campaign play. The Ducat change really forces you to think about what you want to include and to boil down your list to only the most vital units and pieces of Battlekit. There is no frivolity allowed, even more so than in a typical New Antioch list. The Glory changes allowing you to bring Mercenaries mean you can fill in gaps as you see fit, but the downside is that losing them hurts a lot.

If you want to try a unique way of playing New Antioch, give the Papal States a try, and bring the might of the Supreme Pontiff straight to the front lines!

title: The rarest and most expensive Lorcana cards of 2026
content:
What are the rarest, most expensive Lorcana cards? When the characters and films are so beloved by so many, it only makes sense mega-fans are prepared to shell out for a rare Disney card with unique art of their favorite character. This guide covers all the most expensive Disney Lorcana card sales from the most recent sets.

Disney Lorcana may be the newest of the big trading card games, but it has a dedicated fanbase of collectors who will pay a princess' ransom to get their hands on the most coveted cards. Older TCGs may have higher price ceilings - nothing on this list can match the most expensive rare Pokémon cards or expensive Yugioh Cards - but there are some very valuable cards nonetheless! The most expensive Lorcana cards are:

Elsa, Spirit of Winter (Enchanted) - $935

The original Elsa from 2023's The First Chapter set is already a collectible card, but this full art Enchanted variant is in another league. She's a double threat - not just one of the most popular Disney characters of all time, but the first card printed of that character when the game launched. If you've got one, don't let it go…

Pocahontas - Peacekeeper (Iconic) - $982

The incredible multi-colored foiling on this card really does paint with all the colors of the wind. Pocahontas has never looked so noble - or so snug in that gorgeous coat!

Hades, Looking for a Deal (Iconic) - $984

This is currently the rarest Disney villain card around! Though released alongside the previous Pocahontas in winterwear, and just as rare, this card took a lot longer to rise to the heights. Maybe it's because Hades isn't a princess? Still, this sneaky backstabber spent all of August closing the distance, and finally overtook her just before the month ended.

Moana, Curious Explorer (Iconic) - $1,159

Moana was a surprise appearance in Winterspell, a set with a Winter theme, and it seems this explorer's curiosity is so great she didn't have time to dress for the colder weather. Nevertheless, this paper-cut inspired artwork is absolutely adorable, and helps to make this Iconic card so legendary.

Winnie the Pooh, Hunny Wizard (Enchanted) - $1,341

The colors here are making us so hungry. Pooh Bear doesn't have any fancy abilities to show off, but he does have a soothing smile, a fancy cloak, and golden, sugary goodness surrounding him. Those base stats aren't too shabby, either. By the end of August, Winnie the Pooh was getting close to Ariel, after a long time jockeying for position with Moana.

Ariel, Ethereal Voice (Iconic) - $1,344

This ghostly 'Whisper' of Ariel from the Whispers in the Well set not only has a commanding performance, she also commands a high price on the secondary market, which has only crept up since she released.

Lilo and Stitch, Fun-Loving Friends (Iconic) - $1,674

There's so much energy and mischief in this Lilo and Stitch card. It looks like the box art for a straight-to-DVD sequel to the classic movie, and we mean that with love: there's no way any actual animation could live up to the sheer action this promises!

Merida - Formidable Archer (Iconic) - $1,844

We all know that Lorcana is a pacifist game, and nobody involved in a challenge is ever hurt - but we have to wonder what Merida does with her arrows to keep her opponents from getting hurt! This is one of the most dynamic princes poses in all of Lorcana - and one of the few princesses to ever cost more than Minnie Mouse (though the royal rodent has since regained her throne).

Belle and Beast, Certain as the Sun (Iconic) - $2,130

A card as romantic as this was destined to be sought after - Belle and Beast waltzing is a timeless scene from the film that kicked off the Disney Renaissance.  They're also remarkably faithful to their original on-screen appearance as well.

Minnie Mouse, Sweetheart Princess (Iconic) - $2,244

When the first Iconic cards were created for Lorcana they were immediately way pricier than anything else on the market, and nearly made it into the all-time top 10, up against extremely rare early promos. Minnie, blowing a kiss in her medieval princess garb, was beginning to slip from her initial high position on the list - but made a recovery in late August as a sheer lack of supply drove up the market price.

Mickey Mouse, Brave Little Prince (Iconic) - $3,035

But, of course, Mickey was always going to do better than Minnie. So far, this card bucks the Lorcana card trend, with its price and hype only rising over time. It was sitting just at around $2,500 at the start of August, but there are precious few copies in circulation and the market price is now over $3,000.

Buzz Lightyear, Jungle Ranger (Iconic) - $3,632

The price for Buzz Lightyear has practically gone to Infinity and Beyond! When Wilds Unknown released it quickly became the second most valuable card you can open in a booster pack - and now it's surged ahead of the iconic Mickey Mouse. At the time of this update it has reached a plateau and is wavering around the $3,600 mark - perhaps because the best quality copies of the card have found their forever homes, leaving only cheaper versions on the market.

If you're a Lorcana collector but not yet a player, you should fix that immediately! It's easy to learn, and we can talk you through which Lorcana starter decks are worth playing.

title: Gundam Assemble Official Core Rulebook - The Tabletop Battles Hot Take
content:
Lynn: Wait, where am I? There’s a hex map here, and giant robots, but this isn’t BattleTech?

Jake: Alternatively, where am I? There's a hex map, models, and cards but this isn't Underworlds?

Lynn: No, on Thursday Bandai dropped the Official Core Rulebook v1.0 for their hotly anticipated miniature wargaming debut, Gundam Assemble, making it available as a free download from the game’s official site. I’ve been a fan of the Gundam franchise since before I knew what a “MechWarrior” was, and I have most of the launch wave of Gundam Assemble product on preorder with my FLGS, so I’m eager to dig into these rules… and Jake is busy today, so I’ve gotten the chance to do so! Well, he was busy when I wrote that!

Jake: I'll always make time for hexagon-based games! This is an exciting expansion upon the previously published Quick-Start Guide over on the Gundam Assemble website. These rules, alongside the announcement earlier this week that stores will be receiving Learn to Play kits a full month before the general release of the game, mean that we are even closer to getting to play this hotly anticipated game.

While this is our first look at the official rules, there's surprisingly not that much that hasn't been seen before if you've been following the game's progress. Between the Quick-Start Guide and the gameplay demo on the official YouTube channel, a lot of the game's framework has been known for a few months. What this document does do is give us a little more insight and help answer lingering questions. What exactly are the rules for making a team and building a deck? What are the various weapon abilities? And what the heck do Minovsky Particles do? If any of those questions have been keeping you up at night, you should get a sleep study done but you can also find the answers in this document.

Lynn: Now, there’s still a ton of unknowns about this game - most notably, we haven’t seen locked-in final text for any game cards outside those featured in example diagrams in the Core Rulebook - but this is by far the biggest chunk of meat we’ve gotten so far to whet our appetite for speculation. I’m going to read these tea leaves as best I can, but do keep in mind that we’re going off the same publicly-released information you and the rest of the internet are looking at, so our perspective is definitely incomplete.

With that caveat out of the way, let’s take a closer look!

Gundam Assemble Models, Heroic Beginnings starter set. Credit: Greg Chiasson

Presentation

Lynn: The layout of this rulebook is simplistic, with strong “Word document converted to PDF” energy. The title page looks like a placeholder, and art is only present in the form of illustrative diagrams, nothing’s there purely for flavor. The text hasn’t even been organized to ensure clean page breaks; on occasion there are boxed text examples which continue across a page break, lonely headers at the bottom of one page with their section starting on the next page, etcetera.

That said, the illustrative diagrams and examples of play read clearly, and there’s enough of them to cover a lot of scenarios, getting out ahead of some edge case questions and even highlighting a few non-obvious synergies (Duel Gundam and Oggo? Name a more iconic duo!). The writing tries to keep its tone on the “technical writing” end of rules text, with rare intrusions of Bandai marketing lingo, and I’d say it mostly succeeds at that, aside from one or two glaring oversights, which we’ll circle back to later.

Jake: Strongly agree that the layout feels more like a draft version of the rules than a final product, especially when you compare it to the previously mentioned Quick Start Rules. The glossary is also serving double duty in being both a glossary of terms presented earlier in the rules and also a place where a handful of rules are introduced for the first (and only) time. That seems to be an oversight that will hopefully be addressed. I have no idea when that would be, though. Given the delay in having materials printed and boxed up, I'm assuming this is more or less what we'll be getting as a rulebook inside of the boxes that are released in October.

That said, what it lacks in graphical pizzaz, it makes up for with copious examples. In particular, I was pleased to see multiple pages of different examples for determining Line of Sight.

Lynn: On the whole, while there’s no flash here, there is substance, and that’s the part that’s most important for actually getting this game in motion.

Jake: Oh yeah, there's also the glossary at the back. As expected, it serves as a quick reference so you can look up game terms and get definitions. However, this particular glossary also includes a fair number of items that aren't mentioned anywhere else in the rules which feels odd. Mechanics like Challenge, Remote Weapon Systems, and Repair show up here without ever being mentioned earlier in the book. Likewise, a lot of keywords such as Fueled, and Reinforcements get detailed in the glossary without also being mentioned earlier in the book. I think it could really benefit from one more organizational pass.

Lynn: As I'm editing this article, I could totally smooth over the part where Jake mentions that the glossary serves double duty twice, but the irony is too delicious for me not to leave it in. ( ^3^)~<3

Gundam Assemble Miniatures, Wings of Advance starter set. Credit: Greg Chiasson

Revelations

Pre-Game

Lynn: We get some clarified definition of what listbuilding looks like here. Depending on the scenario being played, your squad in a game of Gundam Assemble will typically consist of either three or five units, and your force may include a carrier if (and only if) specified. As previous material has suggested, basically the only limitation on squad creation, outside narrative scenarios, is that you can’t take exact duplicates of any unit which doesn’t have the “Mass-Produced” tag; beyond that you’re welcome to field three different RX-78 Gundams, three different Char Aznables, a tag team of the Wing Zero, Duel Gundam, and an Oggo, or whatever other mad mélange of mobile suits strikes your fancy.

Jake: I genuinely can't wait for Team Chars. Also, going off the section on carriers, players will be able to pick which ones they want to use outside of narrative scenarios that choose for you. I assume this means we'll eventually have a pool of different carriers to pick from and not be limited to White Base vs White Base mirror matches. (Lynn: In fact, already announced releases include a Musai-class for Zeon and the Archangel for the Seed-heads in attendance.)

Lynn: You’ll also build a deck of exactly nine tactics cards (or exactly [number of phases played x 3 + 3], if you want to play past the typical two-phase game length), with your deck-building options constrained by the squad you’ve chosen to take. Every unit has a Signature Tactics card associated with only that specific unit (e.g. only that specific flavor of RX-78, or what have you) which can only be included in your deck if you’re fielding that unit and which can only be used by it, and other cards may be specifically limited by other keywords (with the examples given all being faction tags like “Earth Federation,” “Zeon,” etc.). You can’t include multiple copies of any particular tactics card, and there doesn’t seem to be any carve-out for “mass-produced” tactics like there is for units.

This deck construction mechanic ensures that you can’t see all the cards in your deck without access to additional card draw (something the rulebook does suggest is a mechanic that exists), since you only draw three per Phase of play (so you’ll draw six out of your nine in a standard game). That should be a balancing mechanism, of sorts… even if the Sekiha Love Love Tenkoyken card, or what have you, is absolutely busted good, you can’t guarantee you’ll see it in any given game, and even if you do, you only get to use it once.

Jake: Coming from a game where you built a small deck without duplicates or any guarantee of seeing every card in your deck, this feels oddly familiar. Barring any external card draw, you'll see 66% of your deck in a matchup if you're playing the standard 2 phase game. This is enough to build some reliability into your deck, especially once the card pool builds up a bit.

Looking at the product lineup on Bandai's website makes it seem like we're going to get roughly three tactical cards per model in each product. This works out nicely given that you're going to have three models in your force and a nine card deck. However, the Deluxe sets weirdly only show that they include a single tactical card. I suspect this is a mistake because having 13 models and only one tactical card doesn't make a lot of sense.

Lynn: Look, you can all share that tactics card and you’ll like it!

Terrain

Lynn: While I believe we got water rules somewhere along the way prior to this, the Core Rulebook is our first look at what spaaaace brings to the table. Debris Fields have… the exact same mechanics as water, on the face of it, slowing movement initiated within the terrain and penalizing attacks made against targets inside a Debris Field or by units inside a Debris Field (with the penalties stacking if both the attacker and target are in Debris Fields, even if it’s the same field). Given the penchant of Zeon and its analogues (looking at you, ZAFT) for deploying an entertainingly diverse array of amphibious mobile suits, we’ll probably see individual units which interact with Water differently than they do Debris Fields, but in terms of core rules, they’re the same.

What isn’t the same are areas affected by Minovsky Particles. These don’t affect movement, but impose a (non-stacking) -2 Accuracy penalty when targeting any non-adjacent unit when either the attacker or the target is inside a Minovsky Particle field. From what we’ve seen of the map included in Deluxe Set 01, that can mean a very big chunk of the battlefield applies a heavy nerf to basically all ranged combat in certain scenarios, which… should certainly help in forcing canon-typical knife beam saber fights, I suppose!

Jake: I think it's amusing that Minovsky Particles, a plot device made up to ensure cinematic battles with mobile suits in the anime, wind up being implemented in such a faithful way. You're going to get up close to smash each other and like it.

Gundam Assemble Miniatures, Zeon's Rush starter set. Credit: Greg Chiasson

Carriers

Jake: Carriers were shown in even the earliest of preview images, although they've undergone some visual changes. They've had a few different layouts of the hexes on their base – from a straight line of three hexes to a more Y-shaped five hex base to a four hex diamond. It remains to be seen what they'll look like in the final version of the game. (Lynn: Though I'd say that the wording of these rules implies the "straight line of three hexes" base.) Regardless of what the production version of their bases look like, carriers have a few funky rules and their own section of the rulebook devoted to them.

When moving a carrier, you have to decide if it's moving forward or backward. Whichever direction you choose, that hex of the base moves one space and then the middle hex of the base has to wind up in the hex just vacated by the moving section. Yes, this is wordy and sort of introducing facing in the game when it doesn't come up anywhere else. It feels like it'll be pretty intuitive once in play, though.

Attacking with a carrier has some special rules as well, because all attacks originate from the front hex. You'll need to make sure you're doing sick drifts if you want to swing around an obstacle to get line of sight on targets. It also means the butt of the carrier will block their own line of sight. Sneaking up on the vulnerable section of a carrier feels like it'll be a valid tactic.

In the scenarios that use carriers, they double as the spawning point for your units when they're (re)deployed. They're also units with stats that can be attacked, so what happens if they're destroyed? It turns out they're disabled. This means they can't move, attack, or contest objectives but they still exist on the board as a deployment space.

Lynn: One additional constraint on the movement of carriers is that all the hexes they occupy need to be at the same elevation at the end of movement.

Jake: Oh yeah, that's going to really limit where carriers can be on the maps especially since so far they all seem to have a fair bit of elevation variation.

Push, Pull, and Collision

Jake: Another revelation is the inclusion of mechanics for pushing and pulling models. The implementation is fairly straightforward in that pushes force the model to move away from whatever is pushing it while pulling drags it toward the source. If it's a multi-hex push or pull, then every individual hex has to be further or closer as relevant.

One fun bit is that if you can't be pushed or pulled due to an intervening model or terrain, it causes collision damage. We're out here shoving mobile suits into each other! Any time collision damage occurs, it inflicts two points of damage on everyone involved. So if something is shoved into terrain, the unit suffers two damage. If two models wind up bumping into each other, they both suffer two damage.

Lynn: Also worth noting, some scenario objectives can be picked up by your units, and being Pushed or Pulled (or Dashing, but at least you’re the one who decides whether you do that!) automatically causes you to drop an objective you’re holding! Based on things I've heard from our Crisis Protocol friends, I’d imagine that mobile suits which can force movement will be a very strong inclusion for certain scenarios.

TP-007B Zaku II. Credit: Fowler

Clarification Needed

Jake: As expected for a brand new game, there's a lot going on in this document. It covers the bases pretty well, but we noticed a few places where it would benefit from some clarity. I'm hoping at least one more version of the rules is published with the game's release (version 1.1, perhaps) but failing that we could at least be well served with an FAQ.

One thing that jumped out to both Lynn and myself was that nowhere in the rules document does it mention whether you can shuffle around the parts of your turn. In my own reading, it felt a lot like it was implying you would need to Advance before you could do any of your options for Primary Actions. This goes directly against what has been shown in the Quick-Play Guide where it mentions you can perform an Advance, do a Primary Action of choice, use Command abilities, or play a Tactics card in any order.

Lynn: This is particularly important if you’re planning to Advance and Dash and need to change elevation as part of that movement. Let’s say you’re two hexes away from a two-level-high elevation change, and you need to get up there. If you can Dash, then Advance, you can Dash the two hexes to be adjacent to the cliff and then use the three movement of your Advance to scale the elevation change, but if you need to Advance first and then Dash, you simply can’t cover that same distance.

Another aspect which seems unclear to me is whether you can pay Timeline costs which would carry your token past the end of the second Phase. It’s described that if you go off the end of the Timeline, you loop back around and finish paying the cost by moving additional spaces from the start of the Timeline… in other words, if you spend 4 Timeline when you’re two spaces from the end of the Phase One Timeline, your next action will be two spaces into Phase Two. But can you spend time that’s never going to be played, if you’re near the end of Phase Two (and thus the entire game)? I just don’t know.

Jake: There are also a few places that seem to sport errors of things changing in testing but not being updated in the document. One of these was on page 40 when it's talking about which model can play a Signature Tactics card. The example calls out Epic Shot being usable only by "Hero of Side 7" but the card pictured doesn't have that indicator on it anywhere. Instead, it lists "Legendary Hero." I assume this is something that changed at one point in testing but didn't get corrected in this iteration of the document.

Lynn: Jake and I were both confused for a bit by "Legendary Hero," as well. We initially interpreted it as a "this is unique" marker, the way "Legendary" is used in Magic: the Gathering; it wasn't until I noticed that the Wing Gundam Zero and Buster Gundam cards seen in the rulebook have different descriptors in their black-background keyword tag ("Wing of Destruction" and "Longshot," if you're curious) that I realized "Legendary Hero" was actually the specific descriptor for that iteration of Amuro's RX-78-2!

Speculation

Lynn: The… I’d say yellow flags around game balance are still on display here. Aside from what I assume is the starter box’s RX-78 card, we see unit cards for the Oggo, Wing Zero (Endless Waltz), Guntank, and Buster Gundam. The Buster Gundam is somewhat incomplete, since it comes with interchangeable weapon cards for the Anti-Armor Shotgun or Hyper Impulse Long Range Sniper Rifle and those aren’t seen here, but looking at the other four… the Wing Zero, in particular, has some ridiculous potential (including the innate ability to passively double the range for scoring critical hits?!?), and the Guntank also seems to project serious threat (how does a Range 7, Strength 9 attack which ignores LoS sound?). It’s hard not to feel like relative punching bags like the Oggo will be relegated to narrative play.

Of course, from a lore and vibes perspective, of course Wing Zero is going to stunt on a friggin Oggo; I’m just less sure the whole “any three bodies, no points” approach is going to work for the competitive play we’re theoretically going to see for this game.

Jake: There are certainly plenty of balance levers available to (theoretically) make it work. Between adjusting the victory points for killing units, the timeline costs of their abilities, and the cards available it should (again, theoretically) be possible to balance three headline Gundam suits against three generic Zaku IIs, but I have been playing games long enough to be at least a little wary of how it'll turn out.

Lynn: It is worth remembering that the flashy super attacks I’m worrying over both have a Timeline cost of 4, so you’d see them a maximum of… roughly five times a game, and that’s if the unit in question never dies and never has to do anything with a Timeline cost other than shoot, which seems unlikely.

Jake: Given how important the scenarios seem to be in gameplay, it's hard to form solid opinions without having some of those to work with. There have been some teasers dropped here and there for the first few product releases, but I really want to sit down with the actual scenarios. Going off some earlier reveals, we're going to have the two scenarios from the Starter Box to work with for a few months before more get introduced. I'm particularly interested in the Scenario Pack 01 that is slated to come out in Feburary 2027, especially because it's supposed to be aimed at the more competitive organized play format.

Lynn: My biggest question mark regarding scenario play are the Garrisons. These only have 1 HP, and your opponent scores the same amount of VP for shooting your Garrison from any range that you do by “Rescuing” an adjacent friendly Garrison. At first blush I feel this seems absurdly balanced in favor of killing the enemy over rescuing friendlies, but I might feel differently in play? And certain deployment maps might affect that? We’ll see.

Jake: It turns out war is hell. Blowing up garrisons is easier but just as rewarding as protecting them.

Lynn: AoE effects seem like something that’s going to need to be monitored closely. In particular, given how they’re carried out (one Strength pool is rolled, then the results are separately applied to each target), a buff to Strength which would apply to any target is applied to the entire attack, even though Accuracy modifiers from terrain and the like apply to each target separately, which could lead to some heinous buff interactions if the devs aren’t careful.

I’m spending this section fretting, though, so I should also say that I’m heckin' excited to see what Gundam Assemble has in store for us. I’m already impressed by the game’s roster mixing in deep cuts amongst the obvious stars (I can guarantee you I have never before typed “Oggo” this many times in a day), and there is so much depth this game could mine if it finds its footing for a long production run. I’ve got the majority of Wave 1 on preorder, and I can’t wait to see what squads I can put together and get to smashing my anime war dollies against each other!

Demo game from GAMA. Credit: Fowler

Overall Vibes

Jake: There are definitely a lot of cool mechanics on display here and a solid framework of underlying rules. The timeline continues to impress me as a game system. The way "respawning" works to keep both players involved in the game sounds like it might address some blowouts that happen in similar systems. Being able to pick your custom team out of the whole arsenal of Gundam IPs is great!

That said, I'm with Lynn in that I'm seeing some yellow flags depending on how the game is handled after release. The way cards are being packaged in with various releases immediately brings to mind the early days of Warhammer Underworlds where players who wanted to play a certain set of models were still heavily incentivized to purchase unrelated releases just to add to their toolbox of generic cards. There's also the issue that mass produced units can be fielded multiple times. If someone really wanted to run a full force of a mass produced unit that's only available in one of the $100+ sets, they're going to have to shell out $300-$500 just to do so. That's an awful lot just to run three to five RB-79 Balls.

The initial release cadence is also quite rapid. There are currently 15 different releases from October 2026 to February 2027. On the one hand, this rocks because that's a ton of little robots to collect, build, paint, and play with. On the other, that's an awful lot of stuff to try and keep up with if you want to play this as your "main" game.

I hope the developers are aware of these pitfalls and willing to address them. Particularly because I'm eager to get my hands on the game and play! I feel like it'll be a wonderful addition to a game library, especially if it plays out as quickly as I suspect it will.

Lynn: This looks to me like a relatively casual, beginner-friendly wargame, perhaps even a game to be enjoyed with the fabled “beer and pretzels” (or ramune and pocky, as you prefer)!

There are aspects of the mechanics that excite me… like Jake said, the Timeline is pretty clever, but for me the standout might be the Jumping mechanics, which really feel like they get the vibe of Gundam movement right: If you start from an elevated position and move to a hex at the same elevation, you treat that as perfectly level movement, no rolls to see if the jump succeeds, no extra costs, and you can freely move over enemies that are on lower elevation. If you jump upwards to an even higher elevation, you only pay the difference between your current elevation and the elevation you’re jumping to; you don’t have to climb down and climb back up. In Gundam, a franchise where rocket-boosting around is commonplace enough even the Guntank can do it, this feels only right and proper.

Despite the “gamey” abstractions in the system (some of which, like the respawn mechanic and the “Upgrade” pick-ups, really kind of rub me the wrong thematic way), this does look like a labor of love, even from the limited exposure I’ve had to the game’s cards so far. I think this game looks likely to translate the feel of its mobile suits pretty well, even if the actual scenarios might look a bit more like a computer simulation than a life-and-death struggle to me.

While I could be proven wrong, I don’t have high hopes for the competitive balance of this game, and honestly, that feels kind of freeing for me. Readers who’ve explored my other content will know that I’m a fiend for competition in BattleTech, but it’s comforting to imagine that I won’t end up a cutthroat competitor buying SEED expansions I don’t want to chase meta cards here, and I can just have a bit of fun watching Suletta fight Zechs every so often.

This feels like the place where there’s going to be a smash cut to me-six-months-from-now taking a SEED squad to a tournament or something; we’ll see how things go. ^_^;

I want to say a sincere thank you to my co-author Jake for his continuing coverage of this game, and I hope to see all you Gundam guys, gals, and non-binary pals again in the not-too-distant future! Til’ then, Tobe, Gandamu!

title: D&D is getting a spiritual successor to Dark Sun, made by the original creatives
content:
Dragon Kings, a spiritual successor to Dark Sun from the iconic world's co-creator, comes back to crowdfunding in September. This time, the system-agnostic setting is coming to D&D.

Dragon Kings started life as a 1992 Dark Sun supplement, so this is a homecoming of sorts. Developed by Dark Sun co-creator Timothy Brown, it introduced the titular Dragon Kings as the most powerful beings in Athas, Dark Sun's apocalyptic desert world.

Brown left D&D publisher TSR in the 90s, and by 2014, Dragon Kings had developed into its own system-agnostic setting. It's now set in Khitus, a desolate desert world formerly ruled by the Dragon Kings. Sorcery and psionics are rare yet powerful magical forces. Lizard and insect peoples populate the ruins of the world, rebuilding it with blood and bone.

It clearly shares a lot of DNA with Dark Sun, but there are distinctions. As the new book's Backerkit page puts it: "Where Dark Sun told of a world squandered, Khitus is a world grown complacent and now paying for it". "The difference is this: it is not yet too far gone."

Dragon Kings 5e brings several original Dark Sun contributors into the fold. Brown's co-creator, Troy Denning, is on the development team. Former TSR designers Bill Slavicsek and Rich Baker are credited, and key Dark Sun artist Brom is also returning. Strange Owl Games are responsible for publishing.

The new book seemingly offers everything you'd need to play. Six ancestries are promised, along with new DnD classes and subclasses. A gazetteer introduces the setting, and there are 30+ creatures to populate it. The Backerkit page also says there'll be new rules for Psionics - something D&D is also introducing in next year's official Dark Sun revival.

Dragon Kings will be a 5e product (no word on whether that's 5.5e compatible), but it'll also be playable in D&D 2e "for those that prefer to stay in the original system of Dark Sun". The Backerkit campaign launches on September 22.

Want to talk more about D&D, Dark Sun, and tabletop RPGs? We've got nerdy spaces for pretty much everything in the Wargamer Discord.

title: Warhammer 40k hasn't made lore as good as Trench Crusade Carcass Front since 2002
content:
Carcass Front is the first major expansion for Trench Crusade, a narrative campaign box set that comes with two new warbands and a hardback rulebook packed with lore, custom scenarios, and two campaigns. I've got an early sample, and while I'm still finalising my review, but one thing was apparent from the moment I opened the book and started to read - if you're looking for a grimdark setting to get obsessed with, Trench Crusade has just kicked Warhammer 40,000's teeth in.

I'm not going to spend this article shitting on modern Warhammer 40k; I love 40k, and in those areas where the creatives have plenty of freedom, like model design, the novels, the lore for spin-off games like Necromunda, they create genuinely breathtaking work. But the last time I felt like the lore developments in a Warhammer 40k rulebook or campaign supplement actually mattered was during the Gathering Storm campaign in 2017; and as for the last time the lore really astonished me, we're talking third edition, either the Necrons codex in 2002 or the Eye of Terror campaign in 2003.

I had thought that was a product of me getting older and more cynical. Of course I don't feel the same about Warhammer 40k books as I used to. I got into the game last century. I know the Warhammer 40k factions back to front, and I've been exposed to so much more media since then. Reading wargames books is part of my day job, of course 40k doesn't hit as hard. Nothing is going to feel as cool to me as Warhammer 40k did when I was a kid!

Then I read Carcass Front, and it blew my mind. No, that's an understatement - it shot me full in the forehead with an anti-tank rifle and blew my brains out in a fifteen foot splatter zone. Picture me writing this article with a bloody crater where my head should be, blood-caked fingers tapping on my keyboard as my corpse is reanimated by Trench Crusade's sheer psychic aura.

The Carcass Front is one of the most active battlegrounds in the war between the Faithful and the Fallen, a stretch of coastline and mountainous terrain in the Levant north and east of the fortified city of New Antioch. The servants of Allah, Christ, and YHWH have battled the forces of hell here for centuries, and the land is blighted by wreckage from conflicts both material and spiritual.

The book introduces a dozen key locations from the front, each with at least a full page of incredible artwork, and juicy prose written by ex-Warhammer studio author Graham McNeill. Even the most conventional of these locations takes a classic fantasy trope and spins it into something unexpected.

The Vivarium is a mad scientist's laboratory, but it was founded by a renegade order of unauthorised priests attempting to create their own clone of Christ from relics stolen from the Vatican's catacombs. Nineveh Novus is a cursed, ruined city, but it's ruined and cursed because it was "burned from above and below for seventy-two days" after "profaning both heaven and hell".

Then there's the really good shit, like the Sword of God, a monumental railway gun gifted to the Duke of New Antioch by the Sultan of the Iron Wall, now a sand-covered relic since the alchemists who kept its sacred mechanisms functional were withdrawn in response to a growing political feud. Or the Steel Necropolis, a tank graveyard full of the carcasses of both faithful and heretic vehicles destroyed in an engineered flood, the wreckage stalked by a towering entity of broken iron and diesel fumes known as the Tank God.

Beyond even these there's the 'Pillar of Jonah'. This is some gourmet shit, and if you have any plans to acquire this book, avoid the lore videos that will no doubt pop up on your feed until you can read it yourself. I've taken to thrusting the book under my friends' noses with the Pillar of Jonah pages open, and forcing them to read it. About three to five minutes later (depending on their reading speed) they raise their head and in a stunned voice say something like "Fucking hell, that's metal", or "He ate the pope?!".

I've given you the headlines for these locations, and all the descriptions are fairly brief. But McNeill makes every word count. The lore is layered, with histories and mysteries reaching back into the past and far afield, and even into the real world.

The labyrinth of wrecked ships on the Carrion Coast is all that remains of a Papal Fleet dispatched to relieve New Antioch during the year of the Broken Trinity; the lone, superhuman survivor of that disaster now watches over it from an abandoned airship lighthouse - another location on the map - armed with an anti-submarine gun. Baghras Fortress - a real historical castle built to defend the vital Syrian Gate through the Amanus Mountains - was the last holdout of the fallen Templars who unleashed hell on earth. Their skulls are mortared into its highest towers facing towards Jerusalem and the disaster they unleashed.

These locations aren't just cool, they're eminently gameable. Each one suggests several different ways you could turn it into a board. The colossal corpse-sorting warehouse of Domus Demetrius could be a dense dungeon of morgues or a grisly rail depot complete with cadaver-hauling cranes. The Temple of Leviathan is depicted as a ramshackle folk horror altar erected on a D-Day beach, but if you wanted to make a Lovecraftian sunken city out of it that would absolutely work.

Then there's the Path to Leviathan narrative campaign. The great beast Leviathan was once a prime servant of hell, but was cast down in ages past by the almighty. It is said that the faithful will feast on its flesh at the end of days; inspired by these prophecies, the leper priest Blessed Bartolomeo seeks to drag up the Leviathan from the depths, slay it, and devour it. War Priest Charon of the Heretic Naval Raiders seeks to deny the tyrant YHWH's ordained plan. He means to kill the great beast himself, spoil its meat, and assume its mantle within the courts of hell.

That's the set-up, but Bartolomeo and Charon aren't the protagonists - it's up to your warband to actually make this happen. Perhaps serving one of these two masters, perhaps pursuing an altogether different agenda, across five linked scenarios you'll assemble the knowledge, and then the means, to summon and entrap the mighty Leviathan, and - just maybe - slay it. I'll get into what those scenarios actually involve in my full review, but for now, suffice it to say that they rule.

Strands of this plot are seeded all throughout the lore for the setting, but it's very light touch. This isn't a story you read, it's one you take part in during the campaign. It's clear that the shackled Leviathan is just one fucked up thing among many on the Carrion Front.

Graham McNeill wrote just about everything in Carcass Front that wasn't the rules, with input from three other ex-GW veterans, Tuomas Pirinen, Andy Chambers, and Jervis Johnson. The wealth of experience shows through in how well the lore serves its purpose: it's not a story and it's not an encyclopedia, it's a catalyst to inspire you to play wargames. Yet that same light touch, the combination of bayonet-sharp details and fog-shrouded mysteries, make for the most compelling world-building I've read in years.

You can probably guess that this is getting a good review, can't you? That'll be out soon. If you can't wait to talk about Carcass Front, I'd love to see you in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: TheChirurgeon's Road Through 2026, Part 35: A Hobby Intermission
content:
Welcome back, Dear Reader, to my ongoing blog of hobby and competitive play progress through 2026. Last week I answered questions from Tabletop Battles Patrons about my hobby life and the weekly column. This time around well, I'm a bit less disposed than usual. So this week's update is going to be brief.

The reason this week's article is brief is because I'm traveling for business purposes. Yes, despite being CEO of things around here at Tabletop Battles, I occasionally slum it with a day job to make ends meet. And as luck would have it, this week I've been summoned to Paris. Here's me in front of a famous church:

If I don't look super jazzed there, it's because I was walking around while I had to wait for my hotel room to become available. My flight to CDG got in at like 10am and I smelled ripe. Someone asked me later why I didn't go into the office that morning and I told them I was conducting an act of mercy. Also I've been to Paris more than once and I've been to Sacre Coeur several times. So yeah, not the biggest deal, but fun to do.

The funny thing was, there was absolutely a Warhammer store in the area, so I trudged over there to, just to stop in and see what was up. There are other, better stores in Paris I'd love to visit but at the moment this was the only one I felt like walking to.

It was fine. Just a Warhammer store, albeit one without air conditioning, which made it kind of miserable to be inside. That was crazy, because it was pretty pleasant outside - around 80 degrees and breezy most of the day. That said, I ended up buying something: A Defiler for my Chaos Space Marines. Retail price: 115 Euros; cheaper than the US retail price and I'll get another 15% off when I get the VAT refunded. That's a good deal, especially given none of my local stores seem to carry them right now.

I need this one in particular for my Emperor's Children, though I fully expect it will cost 400 points by November. Speaking of which...

Hobby Progress

I'm still working on my Emperor's Children. It's slower going than I'd like, in part because they're super detailed but also because I just have some kind of weird block when it comes to painting them. No idea why I'm like this. I'm making more progress on the Noise Marines and Tormentors, and my plan is to have a completed unit of each by the end of the month. The Defiler is also on my list now, and represents a massive centerpiece model I can add to the army and make look amazing. Having a big centerpiece is really important when it comes to paint competitions.

Right now my list of painted stuff is pretty small:

- Tormentors x7

- Infractors x5

- Lord Discordant

- Rhino

- Daemon Prince with Wings

- 4 noise marines

That's not a lot! I have a lot of work to do, and it starts with finishing the unit of Noise Marines. I've been delinquent on this army and it'll be good to force myself to finish them in time for the Grand Narrative this year.

Otherwise, I need to finish the Forgefiend I started before Dallas. It's mostly done and it'll look good finished; it also figures into the list I want to run for Challenger's Cup, so it's worth putting in a few extra hours to get it over the finish line. I'm honestly proud I was able to get so much done on him in the short time before Dallas, and there's likely to be more left to do than I expect. But finishing another model will make me feel good, so I'll likely knock him out as a quick/easy win after my next model or two from the Emperor's Chidren.

Final Thoughts

That's it for this week. I'll be back next week with more hobby progress and, hopefully, a game under my belt. Or two, even. I need to get some games in before Challenger's cup, especially now that we've seen the latest round of updates in this week's Balance Update. Fun fact: I wrote the Chaos article from that series on the plane Tuesday night. It wasn't particularly fun and hopefully I won't have to do that again, but preview stuff is always a crapshoot.

See you next Thursday.

title: The best Green MTG card got banned, but its deck is still dominating
content:
The recent MTG banlist change brought some much needed changes to a format that was floundering. The axing of two top blue cards was a great bonus, as Izzet has been oppressively powerful for far too long. But it was also great to see the back of Badgermole, a mana-accelerating card that made green decks extremely fast.

However, now that the dust is settling, it seems like green players didn't need the mole after all. Mono-green decks are still number one in the meta, thanks to all of the great landfall cards released over the last couple of years.

There have been lots of great green Badgermole decks since the card debuted in Avatar: The Last Airbender. As Wizards' banlist article mentioned, the meta moved from Ouroboroid decks, to Nature's Rhythm decks, to landfall lists. It was the growing strength of Selesyna decks which overran the field with Practiced Offense that finally tripped the alarm and made WotC swing its banhammer, but green players just went straight back to their landfall strategies.

It turns out Badgermole was no longer a load-bearing element of this deck - in fact, fans were already in two minds about whether it was worth including. The new deck looks extremely similar to the old, relying on Earthbender Ascension to ramp and stack counters, Icetill Explorer to throw down more lands, Sapling Nursery to throw up a wall of trees, and Mightform Harmonizer to force through more damage.

While the deck could use a better two drop, for the most part players have added an extra copy of Esper Origins, thrown in a basic two-mana ramp spell and carried on like nothing changed.

According to Magic.gg, Mono-Green makes up about 13% of the meta right now. The top deck having a less than 15% meta share suggests WotC's bans had the intended effect and Standard is looking a little healthier right now.

There are several strong decks right now, with Dimir Midrange, Izzet Spellementals and 4-Color Control making up the A-tier. There's lots of jostling for a spot in B-tier though. Notably, Orzhov Lifegain looks strong right now, and I'm keen to see if Sultai Reanimator can make a splash.

What are you playing in Standard right now? Share your brews and fantastic plays over on the Wargamer Discord.

title: Zamanora: Ballad of the Witch Brings Slavic & Balkan Folklore to Life in a New Fantasy TTRPG Setting
content:
Eren Chronicles has launched Zamanora: Ballad of the Witch, a new tabletop role-playing game setting inspired by Slavic and Balkan folklore, on Kickstarter. The campaign, which went live on Tuesday, has already surpassed $120,000 in funding within its first day, making it one of the most notable Dungeons & Dragons 5e campaigns of the year.

Zamanora transports players and Dungeon Masters into a world of rural communities, dark forests, and vengeful witches. The setting is designed to support both Wizards of the Coast’s Dungeons & Dragons 5e and 2024 editions, as well as Legend In The Mist, the rustic fantasy RPG from Son of Oak Game Studio that was recently voted the Most Anticipated TTRPG of 2025.

The Zamanora setting draws heavily from Slavic and Balkan folklore, offering players a chance to explore a world where cautionary tales come to life. Players can create characters from fantastical local creatures such as the mischievous Chorts and the spectral Huants. The setting also introduces unique subclasses, including the Bogatyr fighter, Guslar bard, and Hearth-domain cleric, allowing for thematic storytelling deeply tied to the region’s traditions.

Two new magic systems are introduced in Zamanora: Poppet Magic, a manipulative form of spellcasting, and Ceremonial Magic, which enables non-casters to perform magical rituals. These systems provide fresh ways for players to engage with the game world.

The setting features a variety of mythical creatures familiar to fans of Slavic and Balkan folklore, such as the leshy, baba yaga, and kikimora. These beings are joined by a host of other monsters, each accompanied by detailed descriptions and lore.

The Zamanora Kickstarter offers a range of rewards for backers, from digital PDFs to deluxe collector’s editions. Pledge tiers include options for digital content, physical books, and various accessories. The Core, Deluxe, and Collector’s Boxes include items such as dice, a GMless adventure deck, Baba Yaga miniatures, a DM screen, a monster deck, an illustrated slipcase, and a hand-knitted plushie.

A free demo of the Zamanora setting is available for download on the Kickstarter page, allowing potential backers to explore the world before committing to a pledge.

For more information or to support the project, visit the Zamanora: Ballad of the Witch Kickstarter page.

title: New Reinforcements Arrive in Infinity: PanOceania, Yu Jing, Shindenbutai, and Nomads Expand Their Forces
content:
Corvus Belli has introduced a series of new units and expansion packs for its tabletop game, Infinity, bringing additional options to the PanOceania, Yu Jing, and Shindenbutai factions, while also adding the Nomads to the mix.

Kestrel Expansion Pack Beta: PanOceania’s Colonial Forces

The Kestrel Colonial Force is featured in this expansion, showcasing PanOceania’s adaptability in addressing the challenges of space colonization. As a leading power in the Human Sphere, PanOceania leverages its resources to maintain its position, and the Kestrel forces exemplify this approach. Equipped with advanced technology, these units are designed to uphold PanOceania’s strategic interests.

White Banner Expansion Pack Beta: Yu Jing’s Strategic Elite

Yu Jing, often regarded as one of the top powers in the Human Sphere, continues to strengthen its military capabilities with the White Banner Army. This force has demonstrated its effectiveness in conflicts such as the struggle over Svalarheima. Combining cultural heritage with modern technology, the White Banner Army represents Yu Jing’s commitment to achieving its goals through disciplined and strategic action.

Shindenbutai Expansion Pack Beta: Tradition Meets Innovation

On the distant planet of Shinju, the Shindenbutai serve as the military arm of Greater Independent Japan. This force blends traditional samurai values with advanced technology, creating a unique and versatile unit. Tasked with protecting Japanese interests in Shinju’s challenging environment, the Shindenbutai offer players a distinctive option for their armies.

Yu Jing Action Pack and PanOceania Support Pack

The Yu Jing Action Pack provides players with additional units to enhance their armies, reflecting the faction’s combination of cultural depth and technological advancement. Meanwhile, the PanOceania Support Pack introduces specialized units such as the Trauma-Docs and Machinists, which focus on medical support and technical maintenance to keep PanOceanian forces operational.

JSA Support Pack: The Auxiliary Regiment

The Japanese Secessionist Army (JSA) gains new support options with the Tokusetsu Butai, or Auxiliary Regiment. This unit provides essential medical and technical services, ensuring that the JSA’s front-line forces remain effective. The pack highlights the JSA’s emphasis on a balanced approach to warfare, where support units play a critical role.

Nomads Action Pack: A Faction of Free Spirits

The Nomads, known for their independent and unconventional nature, join the battlefield with their own Action Pack. Originating from three massive spaceships that travel the Human Sphere, the Nomads challenge established norms and offer a unique playstyle. Their focus on creativity and adaptability makes them an appealing choice for players seeking a different approach to the game.

title: Vesta Mandate: A Competitive Political Thriller TTRPG Launches on Kickstarter
content:
Storygames Chicago has launched Vesta Mandate, a hard sci-fi political intrigue tabletop roleplaying game, on Kickstarter. The campaign will conclude on March 22, offering backers the opportunity to secure the game in either digital or premium hardcover formats.

Set on Vesta Station, a critical hub between Earth and the Outer Rim of the solar system, Vesta Mandate immerses players in a tense political landscape. A century ago, revolutionaries overthrew the Corporation’s control of the station, but now the Vesta Accords are expiring, and the Corporation is returning with threats of force. As members of the Station’s interim government, players take on the roles of ambitious politicians, each with their own vision for the future. Through scheming, negotiation, and betrayal, they must navigate a web of alliances, secrets, and crises to shape the fate of the colony.

Vesta Mandate is a Powered by the Apocalypse (PbtA) storygame enhanced with mechanics and procedures that introduce competitive elements, transforming it into a political drama. Drawing inspiration from games like Pasión de las Pasiones, Carved from Brindlewood, Blades in the Dark, and The Last Caravan, as well as media such as The Expanse, Andor, Silo, and A Memory Called Empire, the game delivers a compelling mix of hard sci-fi and political intrigue.

Designed for 3-5 players, Vesta Mandate can be played as a one-shot or a long-term campaign. Players assume the roles of cunning politicians, each with a Hidden Agenda—a secret plan that evolves into a large-scale coup or power grab. Balancing cooperation and betrayal, players must navigate Secrets, Bonds, and Schisms while responding to escalating crises that threaten the station’s survival.

The game introduces several innovative mechanics to enhance its political drama. Hidden Agendas allow players to co-create secret schemes with the GM, which grow into game-changing power plays. Each character has a scandalous past, known as Secrets, created by other players, which can be used as blackmail. Relationships are central to the game, with Bonds representing alliances and Schisms reflecting conflicts that can escalate into full-blown disputes.

The game uses PbtA-style Moves to resolve tense moments. Players roll two six-sided dice (2d6) and add bonuses based on narrative questions, a mechanic inspired by Pasión de las Pasiones. High-stakes Machinations allow players to burn Bonds for dramatic, game-altering effects.

The game includes five ready-to-run modules, known as Crises, such as Neural Poisoning, Corporate Espionage, and Water Riots. These modules are designed for minimal GM preparation and can be played individually or as part of a larger campaign. Additional Crises are planned as stretch goals.

Backers can choose from a variety of reward tiers, starting at $7 for a digital PDF of the game. Higher tiers include a premium hardcover zine, illustrated by Tony Tran, and a discounted bundle with City of Blood and Plaster, Storygames Chicago’s previous ZineQuest project set in Gilded Age Chicago.

Modiphius Entertainment has announced the pre-order availability of the Fallout: Factions Core Ruleboo. This new hardback rulebook aims to enhance the Fallout: Factions miniature skirmish game, offering players the tools to create campaigns set anywhere in the post-apocalyptic Wasteland.

title: Wrath of the Wyvern: A Dark Fantasy Solo TTRPG Launches on Kickstarter
content:
A new dark fantasy solo tabletop role-playing game, Wrath of the Wyvern, has launched on Kickstarter. Set in the Umbral Highlands, a land where humanity struggles to survive under the threat of monstrous wyverns, the game casts players as a lone hunter tasked with reclaiming the world from these fearsome creatures. Inspired by Scottish Celtic mythology, the game blends exploration, survival, and tactical combat into a solo RPG experience.

Wrath of the Wyvern introduces a Fate Card system, which replaces traditional dice rolls. This system, powered by the Fury Engine, is designed to create fast-paced, strategic, and cinematic encounters. Players navigate an open-world hexcrawl, making decisions that influence the fate of the Highlands. The game emphasizes replayability, with branching storylines and faction dynamics adding depth to each playthrough.

Combat is a central element, utilizing a custom Tarot-sized card deck to manage attacks, defenses, and special abilities. Players spend Stamina Points (SP) to execute actions and must adapt to the unique behaviors of their enemies. Survival mechanics, such as hunger, exhaustion, and changing weather conditions, further enhance the exploration experience.

The Umbral Highlands are a perilous and richly detailed world. Players will encounter legendary monsters from Scottish folklore, including the Wulver, Ghillie Dhu, and Kelpie, as well as the game’s primary antagonists: the Sons of Rivesk, ancient and formidable wyverns. Each wyvern battle is a multi-phase event, requiring careful planning and strategy.

In addition to hunting wyverns, players can rebuild Crag Keep, the ruined fortress of the Skyfire Order, and recruit allies to aid in their quest. The game also features arcane powers and legendary weapons, offering players opportunities to wield powerful magic and craft unique tools.

Backers of Wrath of the Wyvern will receive a premium package that includes a 140+ page hardcover rulebook, a massive hexcrawl map of the Umbral Highlands, a Wyvern Showdown battlemap, a hero miniature, and access to the Isle of Skye expansion. The game will be available in English, Spanish, Italian, and French, with each translation handled by a native speaker.

The campaign will run until April 3, giving potential backers 28 days to pledge their support.

title: This Monty Python-esque comedy RPG lets you improv as a band of incompetent and dangerously powerful wizards
content:
Hello Wizard I Have a Problem is a new tabletop roleplaying game that allows players to become powerful and incompetent spellcasters.

The upcoming roleplaying game sees any number of players collaborating together to tell a story about a band of chaotic wizards. Similarly to the likes of absurdist, fantastical comedy such as the works of iconic British group Monty Python, alongside the likes of The Mighty Boosh and What We Do in the Shadows, Hello Wizard I have a Problem is all about rapid scenes infused by the strange and unexpected.

Unlike many other tabletop RPGs, Hello Wizard sees its players taking turns to take on the roles of player character and games master. Each scene in Hello Wizard has a single player take the spotlight as their spellcaster, with the goal of impressing their fellow sorcerers with their magic. The active player describes what spells their wizard casts, with the other players acting collectively as a GM and deciding how these spells can go wrong.

Players will use a Problem Generator included in the fantasy RPG’s rulebook as inspiration for what could go wrong with the wizards’ spells, with the book capable of making over “200,000” prompts for possible disastrous outcomes. Once every player has had the opportunity to step into the spellcasting spotlight at least a few times, the game ends and players tally up their ‘points’ - which are decided by a loose improv system - and determine who is the most impressive wizard.

The rules system for Hello Wizard is very straightforward and intended to be easy for players to learn. Setup for the tabletop RPG is also designed to be quick and easy, with players expected to start in little time. The rulebook for the game will contain advice and optional rules players can use to augment their playthroughs too.

Hello Wizard I have a Problem was created by Sam Armstrong, a tabletop RPG designer who has previously made titles such as All Bastard - a fantasy TRPG in which players take the roles of either a band of bragging heroes or the bastards they defeated - and horror roleplaying game Slasher. The artwork for the game was created by illustrator Evlyn Moreau, who has previously worked on RPGs like Liminal High School.

The crowdfunding campaign for Hello Wizard I Have a Problem is on Kickstarter until later this afternoon, with the title potentially being made available on Armstrong’s Itch.io page. A pledge of £8 ($10) will get backers a physical copy of the game in June, alternatively a PDF version is available for £4 ($5).

title: Re-enact Greta Gerwig’s Little Women with this coming-of-age tabletop RPG
content:
New tabletop roleplaying game, Castles in the Air, will enable players to re-enact their favourite coming-of-age stories.

Castles in the Air was inspired by the likes of classic coming-of-age period dramas such as Little Women by Louisa May Alcott - which was adapted into a 2019 film directed by Greta Gerwig and starring Saoirse Ronan, Emma Watson, Florence Pugh, Laura Dern and Timothee Chalamet - and Anne of Green Gables by Lucy Maud Montgomery, which was adapted into a televisions series in 2017 by Netflix.

The upcoming roleplaying game will see players’ characters grow up together from children to adults during the historical era known as the Gilded Age, which took place in the USA from the 1870s to the 1890s and saw an increase in industrialisation, economic growth and migration to the US. Castles in the Air is a collaborative storytelling game in which players construct narratives that centre around the wonders and fears of childhood, before tackling the joys and hardships of adulthood.

Players begin the tabletop RPG as a tight-knit group of children, all of whom have great expectations of their futures and much quieter current lives. In this phase of the story, players develop a shared childhood together by doing the things rural and financially supported kids did during that era: like playing in their local farmlands, swimming in the lakes and watching the stars.

As the player characters grow up, they’ll begin exploring other feelings and ideas that come with age. Characters in the group might develop a crush on someone or form a heated rivalry with one of the other local children. All the while, the player group will grow up together, before eventually reaching adulthood and potentially finding themselves drifting apart as life takes them in different directions - perhaps to only meet once again.

Players will be able to create their characters in Castles in the Air by choosing from a variety of character roles inspired by classic archetypes, such as the troublesome scamp, studious bookworm or spoiled princess. Add onto this a dream, childhood relationships, a family background and a bosom enemy, and players can even create their favourite characters from the likes of Little Women or Anne of Green Gables.

Castles in the Air was designed and written by Melia Carraway, with contributions from co-created by the co-founders of the RPG’s publisher, Storybrewer’s Roleplaying, Vee Hendro and Hayley Gordon, who also co-designed Good Society: a tabletop RPG inspired by the works of Jane Austen.

The crowdfunding campaign for Castles in the Air is on Kickstarter until June 9th, with a pledge of AU$ 99 (£52/$77) getting backers a physical copy of the game in March 2025. Alternatively, players can get a digital version for a pledge of AU$ 34 (£18/$26).

title: Freak War throws Exploding Kittens and Pokémon into a blender for a trading card game you can play at parties
content:
Take the evolving monsters of Pokémon, cross them with the fast-playing chaos of party game hit Exploding Kittens and you end up with something that looks a lot like Freak War, a new party-game TCG that wants to offer the fun battles of trading card games without the effort of learning lots of rules or building a deck.

Freak War is the creation of Nate Galbraith, aka cartoonist sketchnate, who was inspired after watching kids trying to have Pokémon battles using Uno cards, before suggesting they play classic playing card game War (which you might also know as Battle) instead. The result was a mixture of all three, with Galbraith adding a collection of strange creatures to the cards.

Unlike the head-to-head battles of Pokémon, Freak War can be played with up to four (or more) players, who can simply split the shuffled deck between them to play - though there is the option to build your own custom decks if you really want to.

Everyone plays a creature at the same time, with the highest attack level winning the battle. Like Exploding Kittens, the many cards can also introduce various effects that shake things up, including the power to evolve into bigger creatures - Pokémon-style - and equip modifiers to your own or opponent’s cards to boost or reduce their strength.

Whether the players choose a card from their hand or simply flip the top of their deck depends on the mode they’re playing: the more chaotic War, or the more strategic Battle. Both modes can be modified further by King of the Hill and team rules.

If two players draw in attack level, they both discard a card before facing off by playing another creature. The overall winner takes all the cards played and adds them to their win pile, which are reshuffled into the player’s deck - the person who manages to claim all the cards from their opponents, wins.

The weird and wonderful creatures on the cards have a bit of lore behind them, having been created by the emergence of a second sun that mutated familiar animals like rabbits, foxes and fish into muscly fishpeople, a time-travelling tiger, a partying platypus, a dog with a goldfish bowl for a head, a sad bee and a Man Cat that appears to basically be a bloke in a cat costume, among others.

Modifier cards, meanwhile, range from a Super Sword (and a Super Duper Sword) to the power to swap cards with a rival, cancel a modifier or flip coins for the chance of a power boost. Some of the creature effects get playfully meta in the way you’d expect for a party game too, with the scrap-loving Fly Guy gaining power if there’s uneaten food near the players.

As someone who is admittedly tired of many copy-paste or just downright gross party games (looking at you, double-offending Cards Against Humanity clones), I’m fairly charmed by Galbraith’s goofy creations and the sprinkling of chaotic take-that gameplay in the form of a TCG. (The card layout is quite explicitly inspired by Pokémon cards.) Sure, it’s not going to be for everyone, but as something knowingly silly to fill five minutes with friends and family (especially younger players), it looks like solid, breezy fun for $20 a deck. With a bunch of different packs filled with dozens more creatures from buff penguins to cute-looking snails, I’m pretty intrigued just to see Galbraith’s interpretation of the nonsense of modern Pokémon evolutions, too.

Freak War has already passed its fairly modest crowdfunding goal of $10,000 over on Kickstarter, where its campaign will run until June 13th. The game itself is expected to land with backers next June, just in time to take on holiday.

title: New Blade Runner RPG expansion asks how far you’d go for the Replicant Rebellion
content:
A new expansion for the official Blade Runner tabletop roleplaying game invites you to join the Replicant Rebellion.

Blade Runner: The Roleplaying Game is based on the series of films based on Phillip K Dick’s sci-fi novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep.

Blade Runner, the first of these films, was released in 1982 and directed by Ridley Scott. The film sees Harrison Ford play Deckard, a Blade Runner - an officer whose sole purpose is to hunt and eliminate Replicants, or human-looking androids - who is tasked with finding and killing three escaped Replicants. Following on from the original film, Blade Runner 2049 is a sequel directed by Denis Villeneuve and starring Ryan Gosling. In Blade Runner 2049, Gosling stars as K, a Replicant Blade Runner who must follow the trail of a long-escaped Replicant fugitive and investigate the truth behind her death.

Both films take place in the same fictional science fiction universe wherein Replicants were designed and created entirely to fulfil the needs and wants of their human makers. The Blade Runner franchise is known for its cyberpunk aesthetics, as well as grim view of a near-future wherein corporations are able to commit terrible acts without consequence and exploit large swathes of people.

Blade Runner: The Roleplaying Game usually has players taking the roles of Blade Runners within the LA police department during the time period between the first and second films. However, rather than fulfilling their duties as Replicant hunting officers, the next expansion for the sci-fi RPG sees players abandoning their post to join the Replicant Underground.

Replicant Rebellion is a new expansion for the Blade Runner RPG that sees players get recruited into the Replicant Underground, a secret organisation whose goal is to ensure the freedom and liberation of Replicants: whatever the cost.

Players will see themselves become members of the movement - running their own independent crew as they carry out a variety of missions on behalf of the Underground. From laying charges for explosives, sabotaging the Replicant trade and smoking out moles, players must be prepared for all manner of tasks. Members of the group might even find themselves stuck between a rock and a hard place, as they balance their personal morality with the operations of the Replicant Underground.

Both the Replicant Rebellion expansion and the Blade Runner roleplaying game were published and created by Free League Publishing, the studio behind other licensed TRPGs such as the Alien Roleplaying Game.

A crowdfunding campaign for Blade Runner: The Roleplaying Game - Replicant Rebellion will be launched on Kickstarter on May 28th.
